note:
The same phrase is used at Gen. 2:4; 5:1 in the Septuagint. Here it may refer not only to the genealogy immediately following but also to the account of Jesus’ birth or the Gospel as a whole. The Gk. word translated “genealogy” here is rendered “birth” in 1:18. See Introduction: Title.

**Christ.** This title comes from the Gk. word _christos,_ meaning “anointed.” It is the Gk. translation of the Hb. “Messiah”; see note on 1 Sam. 2:10. In the OT, prophets, priests, and kings were anointed with oil (cf. Ex. 29:7; 1 Sam. 16:13; 1 Kin. 19:16). Anointing dramatized the bestowal of wisdom and power from the Holy Spirit, granting an officer the ability to fulfill his calling. The OT promised the coming of the righteous servant of the Lord (Is. 42:1–9), who would be a prophet like Moses (Deut. 18:18, 19), a priest like Melchizedek (Ps. 110:4), and a king like David, the Lord’s anointed (Is. 55:3–5; Jer. 30:9; Ezek. 34:24; Hos. 3:5; Zech. 12:8). Matthew reveals that Jesus is the Christ, the promised king and deliverer.
The specifics of this genealogy differ from the one found in Luke; see note on Luke 3:23–38.

Women are not usually named in ancient Near Eastern genealogies, but they are intrinsic to God’s purpose in sending Christ. The five women named in Jesus’ genealogy all remind us that God often does the unexpected and chooses the unlikely. Tamar (v. 3) reminds us of Judah’s failures (Gen. 38:6–30); Rahab (v. 5) was a harlot (Josh. 2); Ruth was a Moabite (Ruth 1:4) and thus subject to a special curse (Deut. 23:3–5); Uriah’s wife, Bathsheba (v. 6), was David’s downfall (2 Sam. 11). Mary fulfills Is. 7:14 (v. 23) and the even more important promise of Gen. 3:15 (Gal. 4:4). At least three of the five (Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba) have Gentile associations, an important theme in this gospel (2:1–12; 28:18–20).

Matthew organizes the genealogy into three groups of fourteen to show that God has a purpose in history. The early history leading to David, the monarchy leading to the exile in Babylon, and the history of Israel after the exile all lead up to and point to Christ. Jechoniah (Jehoiachin) is included in both the second and third groups of fourteen, whereas three kings (Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah) are omitted from the second group (2 Kin. 8:25–14:22; 2 Chr. 21:4–26:13). Biblical genealogies are selective in order to reinforce theological motifs or to aid readers in memorizing the genealogical data.

verse_quote: Joseph ... resolved to divorce her quietly.
note: In Joseph’s day, engagement is nearly as binding as marriage, and infidelity during betrothal makes divorce virtually obligatory.

God imparted special revelation through dreams to Joseph (also 2:13, 19, 22), the magi (2:12), and the wife of Pontius Pilate (27:19), as He had to OT figures such as Joseph, son of Jacob (Gen. 37:5–11; 40:5–19; 41:1–36).
The Gk. equivalent of “Joshua,” meaning “Yahweh is salvation,” or “Yahweh saves.” Often in names, a shortened form of God’s name is used (e.g., in Elijah, Isaiah, Joshua).

See note on Is. 7:14. Jesus’ conception by a virgin is miraculous, announcing that God is present with His people and will soon redeem them. This quotation is the first of many OT references Matthew uses to show that Jesus fulfills the OT (2:6, 15, 18, 23 and notes). In the entire gospel there are twelve such fulfillment formulas, and more than fifty OT quotations. See theological note “The Virgin Birth” on p. 1782.

**Immanuel ... God with us.** In the OT, God’s promise to be with His people was the answer to their fears (Josh. 1:9; Is. 43:1, 2). His glory dwells in Israel’s midst in the tabernacle. Jesus, the ultimate and complete fulfillment of the “Immanuel” promise, will commission His apostles and encourage His church with the promise, “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

verse_quote: in the days of Herod the king.
note:
Herod the Great is known to have died in 4 B.C. Therefore, Jesus was actually born c. 5 or 6 B.C., according to the standard dating of the Gregorian calendar.

**wise men.** The magi were not kings, but priests or court advisers, like Joseph or Daniel. They were probably from Mesopotamia, the region of ancient Babylon (modern-day Iraq), although other locations east of Palestine have been suggested. There are numerous accounts of ancient astrologers interpreting astronomical phenomena as heralding the birth of kings.

This may have been a planetary conjunction, a supernova, or something purely supernatural (which seems most consistent with its finally coming “to rest over the place where the young child was”; 2:9). Whatever the case, it alludes to the star of Jacob (Num. 24:17), which was prophesied by another Gentile, Balaam.

History records Herod’s paranoia and murderous violence toward members of his family. As an Idumean appointed “king of the Jews” by Julius Caesar, Herod is understandably disturbed by a report that a rival, who is a legitimate heir to David’s throne, has been born.

The second line of the quotation in Matthew appears to say the opposite of the second line of Mic. 5:2 (“too little”), but Matthew is giving the sense of the prophetic text, namely, that though Bethlehem appears to be insignificant, it is in truth important. The religious experts concluded from the Prophets that the Messiah was to be born in Bethlehem, but not one of them bothered to make the short journey with the wise men to see Christ. Nor did Herod, despite his professed desire to show deference to the newborn king (2:8).

Jesus is no longer in a stable at this point (cf. Luke 2:7). This visit is some time after the birth (v. 1), perhaps a year or more (cf. v. 16). Although the wise men likely do not realize the full symbolic value of their gifts, Matthew records them to show the fulfillment of OT passages where the Gentiles bring their wealth to Israel’s king (Ps. 72:10; Is. 60:6).

Hos. 11:1 refers to God’s calling His son Israel out of Egypt in the exodus (see Ex. 4:22, 23). Matthew means that the history of God’s redemption of Israel points forward to Jesus, the true Son of God. When Israel left Egypt, its fidelity as God’s son was tested forty years in a wilderness, and the record of this testing is largely one of failure (Deut. 8:2–5). Jesus is later tested in the wilderness forty days. He sustains His test and shows that He is indeed the faithful Son of God (Matt. 4:1–11).

Matthew is quoting from Jer. 31:15, a prophecy about the exile. Jeremiah uses the imagery of Rachel weeping for her sons Joseph and Benjamin to describe the sorrow of Israel at the time of the exile. In the next section of Jeremiah’s prophecy, he foresees the return from exile, a new exodus. Matthew’s use of this prophecy appears to portray Jesus as a new Moses (the one who led Joseph’s descendants out of Egypt) who fulfills the prophecy of a second exodus. Like Moses, Jesus escapes slaughter as an infant. Like Moses, He is sent to rescue God’s chosen ones.

verse_quote: he would be called a Nazarene.
note: The OT has no verse exactly corresponding to this, but note that Matthew introduces this reference to the prophets in more general terms than his other quotations. Nazareth was Christ’s home, but Matthew’s point is probably that Jesus would be despised, as people from Nazareth were (John 1:46; 7:42, 52). If so, the Scripture in view may be Is. 53:1–3. Alternatively, it might refer to Is. 11:1, which refers to the Messiah as a “branch” (Hb. _netser_) from the roots of Jesse.

The first command of both John the Baptist and Jesus (4:17). Repentance is not just sorrow for sin but a decisive change, a turning away from sin to a life of obedience that flows from trust in God. “Repent” translates the OT call to Israel to “return” to faithfulness to the covenant. It does not mean self-punishment, depression, or mere remorse. Judas was sorrowful and distressed (27:3), but he did not repent. See theological note “Repentance” on p. 1964.

**kingdom of heaven.** The message of John the Baptist introduces the theme of Jesus’ teaching. Mark and Luke call it the “kingdom of God” (4:17; cf. Mark 1:15). In Matthew, “heaven” stands for the divine sovereign who rules in heaven (cf. Luke 15:18).The kingdom or the reign of God is what the OT prophets awaited: God’s display of His sovereignty in the redemption of His people and the destruction of His enemies. John and Jesus proclaim that the time of waiting is over and the king Himself has come. With the death and resurrection of Jesus and the spread of the good news to all nations, the OT promises of God have been largely fulfilled for us, although we still await their complete realization when Christ returns in judgment (ch. 13 and notes).

**is at hand.** The arrival of the promised Messiah means that the age of God’s redemptive intervention in justice and mercy is dawning, giving urgency to John’s summons to turn from sin to God for salvation.
John the Baptist proclaims the coming of the Lord, using Is. 40:3. John’s ministry points forward, like the OT prophets, to a greater One who comes after him (11:7–11; Acts 19:4, 5).

verse_quote: camel’s hair and a leather belt.
note: John’s clothing identifies him as the promised prophet who comes “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (2 Kin. 1:8; Mal. 4:5, 6; Luke 1:17).

Christian baptism is not identical with the baptism of John. Although Christian baptism retains the symbolism of repentance and purification (Acts 22:16; Eph. 5:26), it is performed in the name of the triune God (28:19) and signifies our union with Christ in His death and resurrection (Rom. 6:3–6; 1 Cor. 12:13; Gal. 3:27; Col. 2:12). See note on Mark 1:4.

The OT promised the coming of the Lord in righteous judgment (Ps. 96:13; Zeph. 2:1, 2; Mal. 3:2). John will not allow the leaders to suppose that the cup of God’s wrath is only for Israel’s enemies and that their own nation will escape. John is later puzzled that Jesus does not immediately bring judgment (11:2, 3 and note).
Acts that indicate an inner righteousness, not merely outward conformity. Since the Pharisees consider themselves to be the righteous of their day, the words of John must cut deep.

Although being Jewish includes outward covenant privileges (Rom. 9:4, 5), it is only by an act of God that one can join the true children of God, who are heirs of the blessings promised to Abraham’s descendants (Gal. 3:13, 14, 29; 4:21–31). Only God can change hearts of stone (Ezek. 36:25, 26). Neither a Jew by birth nor a Christian by birth can expect to be spared judgment apart from the fruit that gives evidence of repentance and faith.
Just as the kingdom is imminent, so is judgment; the coming of one implies the other. John does not yet know that Jesus’ immediate task is not to bring judgment, but to bear it Himself (11:2 note).

verse_quote: with the Holy Spirit and fire.
note: Cleansing with fire describes God’s supernatural baptism, contrasted with the symbol of cleansing with water. The fire of the Spirit renews the people of God and consumes the wicked as chaff (Is. 4:4; Zech. 13:9; Mal. 3:2, 3; 4:1). John’s witness to Jesus as the Lord who has come (v. 3) is extended. As Lord, Jesus baptizes with the Spirit and executes the last judgment. See theological note “Baptism” on p. 1988.

John is reluctant to baptize Jesus because he recognizes that Jesus has no need for repentance. But in order for “all righteousness” to be fulfilled, Jesus has to be identified with His people as the bearer of their sins (2 Cor. 5:21). Isaiah foretold that God’s righteous servant would “make many to be accounted righteous” as he was “numbered with the transgressors” (Is. 53:11, 12). Ultimately, John’s baptism points to Jesus, for only Jesus’ death on a cross, which He calls a “baptism” (Luke 12:50), can take away sins. Jesus’ identification with His people includes His baptism and death, His anointing with the Spirit, and His victory over temptation. See theological note “The Baptism of Christ” on p. 1733.

God’s kingdom (His sovereign rule in salvation and judgment) is defined by His righteousness. Jesus teaches the perfect righteousness that God requires (5:20, 48); He also secures God’s righteousness for sinners. His baptism points to His death as “a ransom for many” (20:28) and shows the perfect obedience in which He fulfills all righteousness (Jer. 23:5, 6). Remission of sins and the gift of righteousness are received through faith in Jesus (8:10; 23:23; cf. 21:32). Those who lack God’s righteousness but hunger and thirst for it will be filled (5:6; 6:33). Jesus calls those burdened with the load of self-righteousness to find their rest in Him (11:28–12:8).

The testimony from heaven confirms Jesus’ identification as the royal Son of God (fulfilling Ps. 2:7; cf. Ex. 4:22), who is also the obedient and suffering Servant who pleases the Lord (Is. 42:1).

**3:16 like a dove.** The Spirit’s appearance in the form of a dove reminds us of the Spirit’s creative activity in Gen. 1:2 and may point to the beginning of the new creation through the ministry of Jesus (1:1 note)., 17

Although God Himself tempts no one (James 1:13), our temptations are included in His sovereign plan for our good. If we overcome, we are strengthened; if we succumb, we recognize more clearly our need for further sanctification and grace.

The temptation of Jesus (vv. 1–11) parallels the testing of Israel in the wilderness. The forty days correspond to the forty years of wandering (cf. Num. 14:34). His temptation recalls Deut. 8:1–5, which He quoted in response to one of the temptations. The experience of Israel in the wilderness was the type or shadow of Jesus’ temptation in the wilderness after His baptism.

The temptations appeal to common motivations: physical drives, pride, and the desire for possessions (1 John 2:16). But each is pointed specially at the Messiah. Satan challenges Jesus to prove the truth of the Father’s words at His baptism: “If you are the Son of God” (vv. 3, 6; cf. 27:40). The third temptation offers Jesus a path to kingship that avoids the cross. Jesus was tempted in every way just as we are (Heb. 4:15), but He did not sin. He represents us before God as a “merciful and faithful high priest” (Heb. 2:17), one who knows through His human nature what it is to endure temptation. See theological note “The Sinlessness of Christ” on p. 2203.
See note on 16:16.

In Deut. 8:3, this refers to God’s word of direction in the wilderness and His provision of manna. Jesus will not abandon His trust in God to provide for Himself. Jesus replies to each of Satan’s temptations with a reference to Scripture. The “sword of the Spirit” is God’s Word (Eph. 6:17), and Jesus relies on Scripture for victory in His spiritual struggle. See theological note “Special Revelation and the Bible” on p. 142.
Part of the temple wall overlooked the Kidron Valley, leading to a tremendous drop from the top of the temple wall to the bottom of the valley.

Satan quotes Scripture, but he uses Ps. 91:11, 12 in a way exactly opposite to the original meaning. Ps. 91 is an exhortation to trust in God; Satan attempts to replace trust with a test, casting doubt on God’s faithfulness. Presumption is not a mark of great faith but evidence of no faith at all. See theological note “Satan” on p. 760. The tempter strategically avoids Ps. 91:13 (“the serpent you will trample underfoot”), which alludes to the earliest gospel announcement in Scripture about the defeat of “that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world” (Rev. 12:9; cf. Gen. 3:15).
Jesus rejects idolatry with all the zeal of true worship, quoting Deut. 6:13. He commands Satan to depart, having conquered the “strong man” (12:29).

Matthew stresses Jesus’ focus on the nation of Israel during His earthly ministry (10:5, 6). However, his observation that Jesus’ ministry fulfills Is. 9:2 shows that the commission in Matt. 28:19 to go to the Gentiles is not an afterthought; the ultimate goal of God’s redemption has always included the nations, foreshadowed in the magi’s worship of Jesus soon after His birth (2:2).

This phrase, which also occurs in 16:21, marks a turning point from the period of preparation to the period of Jesus’ public ministry. Its reappearance at 16:21 signals a shift in Jesus’ teaching—from the coming of the kingdom to the suffering of the king.

**Repent.** See theological note “Repentance” on p. 1964.
Of those whom Jesus calls as disciples, Simon Peter, James, and John become His closest circle (17:1; 26:37). Andrew introduces his brother Simon and others to Jesus (John 1:40–42; 12:20–22).

Teaching involves communicating the nature and purpose of God’s kingdom, as seen in the Sermon on the Mount (chs. 5–7) and the parables of the kingdom (ch. 13). Preaching is proclaiming the good news that God’s kingdom is near, that His sovereign purposes in history are finally being realized. Healing, as well as teaching and preaching, are a sign that this kingdom has come (11:5).

In Roman usage, “Syria” applied to virtually the whole of Palestine with the exception of Galilee (cf. Luke 2:2). A Galilean would probably have understood “Syria” to refer to the territory just north of Galilee, from the Mediterranean to Damascus.

**epileptics.** The only other use of this word in the NT is in 17:15, where it is applied to a demon-possessed boy who exhibits symptoms of epileptic seizures.

The Sermon on the Mount is the first of five great blocks of Jesus’ teaching in Matthew (Introduction: Characteristics and Themes). It is the classic statement of the ethics of the kingdom of God. The early church favored a literal interpretation but fully applied the sermon only to special classes of Christians, especially monastics. Others, such as the Anabaptists, have attempted to apply it literally to every Christian, or even to society and the state. Still others have viewed it as a heightening of the law of Moses with the aim of inducing repentance (Luther). Some consider its demands too risky to implement in the present age and expect them to become applicable in a future millennium, when Jesus reigns. Finally, some have argued that the demands of the sermon are not to be understood literally but that Jesus is concerned with inward disposition rather than outward conduct, or that the severity of the sermon is intended to compel a decision by the hearers either for or against God’s demands on their lives.

We must recognize that the sermon is directed to the disciples and through them to the whole church today. The sermon addresses both inward motives and outward conduct (5:21, 22, 27, 28), calling the adopted sons of God (5:9) to reflect the character of their heavenly Father (5:16, 48; 6:1, 6, 9, 32, 33). These legitimate demands set the bar so high (5:48) that no one except Jesus, the king Himself, fulfills them flawlessly. We are therefore driven to the grace and mercy of God both for forgiveness in our failure (6:12) and for the Spirit’s strength when our faith and faithfulness are tried (6:13).

**5:1 went up on the mountain.** Since Jesus reveals the depth of the commands given through Moses, His ascent of a mountain is reminiscent of Mount Sinai. The content of this sermon is similar to the Sermon on the Plain recorded in Luke 6.

**sat down.** It was customary for first-century teachers to sit while teaching (Luke 4:20; cf. Matt. 23:2).

**his disciples.** Although the crowds are mentioned (7:28), Jesus addresses the instructions and promises of His sermon to those committed to following Him and willing to endure persecution for His sake (5:11).

This means more than the emotional state represented by the word “happy.” It includes spiritual well-being, having the approval of God, and thus a destiny of delight in communion with the Creator (Ps. 1).

**poor in spirit.** Every human being (except Jesus) is spiritually destitute in God’s sight, but only those who see this poverty—who mourn over sin and thirst for righteousness—will inherit the kingdom of heaven. Paul notes the same principle in Rom. 9:30, 31. The parallel in Luke 6:20 omits “in spirit.” This has led many to suppose Jesus refers primarily to the materially poor. Material poverty and recognition of spiritual need often go together (Ps. 9:18 note), but financial want does not necessarily produce the dependent humility that receives God’s favor.
The context indicates that these are mourning over sin and evil, especially their own, and over the failure of mankind to give proper glory to God.

This beatitude resembles and is probably based on Ps. 37:11. The meekness in view is an attitude of humility and submission to God. Our pattern for meekness is Jesus (the same Gk. word is translated “gentle” in 11:29), who submits to the will of His Father.

**inherit the earth.** The ultimate fulfillment of the promise to Abraham (Gen. 12:1–3; 13:14–17), whom Paul calls “heir of the world” (Rom. 4:13; cf. Heb. 11:16).
Those who seek God’s righteousness receive what they desire, not those who are confident of their own righteousness (Luke 18:9–14; Rom. 9:30–10:4; Phil. 3:7–9).

God’s mercy is not a reward earned by our showing mercy to others. Rather, those who recognize the magnitude of the mercy He has shown them will treat others as their Father has treated them (see 6:14, 15).

Because God is spirit, His divine essence is invisible (John 4:24; Col. 1:15; 1 Tim. 1:17; 6:16). Because He is infinitely holy, sinful humans would be destroyed if they were to behold His glory directly (Ex. 33:18–23). Nevertheless, believers “see” God through the insight of faith, and Jesus assures His disciples that in seeing Him, they have “seen the Father” (John 14:9). In the glorified state, God’s children will “see him as he is” (1 John 3:2; Rev. 22:4).

Conflict among individuals, races, and nations comes from our alienation from God. Jesus is the great peacemaker through His wall-destroying death (Eph. 2:14–18). In vv. 44, 45, Jesus calls the children of God to make peace, even with their enemies.

The primary value of salt is not as a flavoring but as a preservative. Disciples are to hinder the world’s corruption. The salt deposits along the Dead Sea contain not just sodium chloride but a variety of other minerals as well. This salt can become useless when the rain washes out its saltiness over the years. Likewise, Christians whose value and conduct do not remain distinct from the culture around them fail in their mission.

In Is. 60:1–3, God promised that the light of His glory in Israel would attract all nations. Jesus is the light of the world (John 1:9; 8:12), and His light now shines through His church (1 John 1:8–10).

A way of referring to the whole OT.

**not come to abolish ... but to fulfill.** The correctives of vv. 21–48 should be read in light of this opening remark. In fulfilling the law, Jesus does not alter, replace, or nullify the former commands; rather, He establishes their true intent and purpose in His teaching and accomplishes them in His obedient life. The Law, as well as the Prophets, points forward to Christ. See theological note “The Law of God” on p. 124.

The smallest letter in the Gk. Alphabet (iota), and a tiny extension that distinguishes certain letters in the Hb. Alphabet (dot).

**until all is accomplished.** The full manifestation of God’s kingdom (chs. 24; 25) for which believers are to pray (6:10).

Jesus does not criticize the Pharisees for their strict observance of the law but for their emphasis on outward conformity to it without a proper inner attitude. By focusing on externals, they avoid the real intent of the law and so obscure its real demands (23:23–28). The Dead Sea Scrolls refer to the Pharisees as “seekers after smooth things” because they accommodated and compromised the law to fit the realities of life. Such accommodation removed awareness of the need for grace and dependence on God. In the following verses, Jesus restores the true nature of God’s law as demanding total and radical holiness. Jesus demands a deeper obedience, not disregard of God’s commands.

verse_quote: You have heard that it was said.
note: Refers not to the teaching of God’s law itself, with its promises, but the teaching of the law by scribes and Pharisees (v. 43 note).

Apparently, Jewish law had sanctions against the specific insult _raca,_ but Jesus shows that any verbal abuse makes one liable to eternal damnation.

**hell of fire.** Gk. _Gehenna,_ the “valley of Hinnom,” was a trash dump outside Jerusalem where fires burned constantly. It was notorious as the location of human sacrifices by fire during the reigns of Ahaz and Manasseh (2 Chr. 28:3; 33:6). Jeremiah called it the “Valley of Slaughter,” an appropriate symbol of God’s fearful judgment (Jer. 7:32). See theological note “Hell” on p. 1753. Jesus uses this site as a metaphor for perpetual physical and spiritual torment awaiting the wicked.

While vv. 23, 24 deal with the reconciliation of an offended brother, vv. 25, 26 appear to address the problem of conflict in larger society—in this case, legal conflict. Christians are to work for reconciliation in all areas of life (Rom. 12:14–21).

The severity of the demand illustrates the radical nature of Jesus’ ethic and our radical need. Sin against God must be avoided at any and all costs. Jesus is not advocating self-mutilation. After all, lust does not come from the eyes or hands but from the heart and mind (15:19). Christians must avoid not only the physical act of adultery (“hand”) but also those thoughts and fantasies that lead to a lustful attitude (“eye”).
See 19:3–10 and notes; theological note “Divorce” on p. 1755.

Some have understood Jesus’ prohibition of oaths to be universal, but Jesus Himself submitted to an oath (26:63) and Paul invoked God as his witness in Rom. 1:9. God Himself takes an oath so that we might be encouraged (Heb. 6:17). Jesus is addressing a narrow and misleading legalism that requires a specific oath to make spoken promises binding, implying that trustworthiness in speaking is optional when unaccompanied by a solemn oath. Jesus demands an integrity in speaking such that everything is spoken as though it is under oath. He also prohibits the implicit idolatry of swearing by anything less than God. See theological note “Oaths and Vows” on p. 717.

The original intent of Ex. 21:24; Lev. 24:20; and Deut. 19:21 was to limit punishment to that which is equitable, fitting the crime. These limitations prohibited exacting a greater vengeance (such as Lamech boasted in Gen. 4:23, 24) or having different penalties for different social classes. Jesus contradicted those who saw in this principle grounds for personal vengeance.

In context this means “Do not seek restitution in court.” The slap on the right cheek is a backhanded one—an insult as well as an injury. Jesus’ remarks may refer back to the words of the servant of the Lord in Is. 50:6.

The possibility of a Roman soldier coercing a person to serve as a guide or burden carrier was real. Even if compelled by force to do something for someone, one can demonstrate freedom by volunteering more than is demanded rather than begrudging the service.

This is not in the OT but was a false conclusion in scribal teaching drawn from the narrow understanding of “neighbor” as simply one’s fellow Jew. Jesus shows that the true intent of Lev. 19:18 extends even to one’s enemies (Luke 10:29–37). In the same chapter of Leviticus, Israelites are called to love the Gentile sojourner “as yourself” (Lev. 19:33, 34).
Those whom God receives by His unmerited grace through His Son Jesus must reflect their Father’s kindness to the undeserving and unthankful. See theological note “Providence” on p. 1045.

The standard that God demands of His people is His own perfect character. God’s perfection includes the love of benevolent grace (v. 45). Although we cannot attain such perfection in this life, it is the goal pursued by all those who have become children of the Father (Phil. 3:12, 13).

Jesus affirms the positive value of such acts, but only when done in submission to God and love for Him rather than for _human_ personal glory. Acts of piety (generosity, prayer, fasting) performed for the sake of public recognition are self-serving and do not show love for God or neighbor.

In the NT, the hypocrite is one who claims to have a relationship with God and to love righteousness but is self-seeking, self-reliant, and even self-deceived. In ch. 23, Jesus will expose the inconsistencies of Israel’s religious leaders, whose deeds contradict their words.
See theological note “Prayer” on p. 1808.

verse_quote: do not heap up empty phrases.
note: This prohibition does not contradict the principle that one should keep asking God for what is believed to be His will (Luke 18) but corrects the idea that God is impressed with quantity of words.

This prayer is a model of brevity, simplicity, and childlike dependence and confidence, asking first for God to be glorified and His purposes to be achieved and then for our own needs.

**hallowed be your name.** Not just that God’s creatures may keep it holy but that God may Himself hallow it by being the holy judge and savior. Reverence for God’s self-revelation is the heart of the third commandment (Ex. 20:7).

The Gk. word translated “daily” is known only from this prayer. It has been understood to mean “daily,” “necessary,” “future,” or “tomorrow’s” bread. There are three basic interpretations for it. The sacramental view is that it refers to the bread received in the Lord’s Supper. Another view is that it symbolizes life in the coming kingdom, making the petition equivalent to “Your kingdom come” in v. 10 (cf. John 6:35–40). A third view takes it as a request for God’s provision for our physical needs. This last view is the best, since this theme is developed in vv. 19–34 (cf. Prov. 30:8).

Spiritual debts—that is, sins—are in view. Christians must forgive others in response to God’s forgiveness (18:32, 33). Those who do not forgive others cannot expect God’s forgiveness for themselves (vv. 14, 15), since a genuine apprehension of God’s grace received will make us gracious toward others.

The forgiven pray this petition because they trust God and distrust themselves. The Father may test us (4:1; Deut. 8:2), but He will not allow us to be tempted beyond our capacity (1 Cor. 10:13; James 1:12, 13).

This symbolized rejoicing (Pss. 23:5; 45:7; 104:15; Is. 61:3), but it was also part of the first-century Jew’s daily routine except when fasting (Dan. 10:3). Not to anoint oneself would advertise one’s self-denial to a human audience.
“Rust” refers not only to the corrosion of metals but also to mildew, wood rot, and the like. Every material thing is subject to decay or loss.

The good eye looks to God as its “master” (v. 24) and fills the person with the light of God’s will. The bad eye looks to “treasures on earth” (v. 19) and admits only the darkness of greed and self-interest. The person’s whole life will be determined by the kind of light the eye lets in.

Anxiety over the uncertainty or scarcity of resources to sustain physical life reveals a faltering faith in the Father’s care for His children. Confident prayer, with thanks, is the antidote (Phil. 4:6, 7).

The point is not that birds are idle but that birds do not and need not worry about what the future holds. Anxious worry changes nothing (v. 27) and shows a lack of trust in God’s knowledge and care (vv. 32, 33). See theological note “Providence” on p. 1045.

verse_quote: seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness.
note: We are to make God’s redemptive rule (3:2) and a right relationship with Him the highest priorities in life (3:15 note). Worry is inconsistent with this priority; its doubts distract from these supreme goals. God will meet all the needs of those who risk all for Him.

Jesus prohibits one kind of judging (or one motive for judging) but approves a different kind. Condemning others for their faults is failure to exercise forgiveness (6:14, 15); only a gentle and humble correction that first recognizes one’s own greater faults (the “log” in one’s own eye) can help. There is also a necessary, discerning kind of judgment that does not condemn but distinguishes unbelief from belief (v. 6). The method of discernment is given in v. 16.

These animals are ceremonially unclean (1 Sam. 17:43; Prov. 26:11; Lev. 11:7). They symbolize people who respond to the priceless message of God’s kingdom (Matt. 13:45, 46) with adamant unbelief. Jesus’ messengers must discern when their gospel message meets obstinate resistance (10:14; 15:14). The book of Acts illustrates this principle in practice (Acts 13:44–51; 18:5, 6; 28:17–28).

**what is holy.** A reference to the gospel and evidences of the kingdom, such as healings and exorcisms.

The general sinfulness of humanity is assumed here, since even those who call God “Father” are said to be evil. Yet by God’s grace, flawed human fathers meet their children’s requests in love. How much more will God the Father, who treats even enemies kindly, answer His children’s prayers.

**good things.** These gifts from the Father are the things Jesus has been describing as necessary for disciples: righteousness, sincerity, purity, humility, and wisdom. Those who know their need will ask God for them. The parallel in Luke 11:13 focuses on the one greatest gift—the Holy Spirit.

Often called the “Golden Rule,” this principle was stated in a negative form by various ancient thinkers as, “Do not do to others what you do not want done to you.” Jesus makes it a positive obligation, a requirement to proactively do for others the good one wants for oneself. Here it appears after the discussion of God’s goodness and His willingness to give.

Presenting a rosy picture of the Christian life and minimizing that it is filled with trouble does not follow the lead of our Lord or His apostles (Acts 14:22; Phil. 1:29, 30). It may be that the “false prophets” of v. 15 are especially those who deny that the way is narrow and hard.

The message of false prophets may be attractive and even seem orthodox. The only way to know for sure is to allow time to see “their fruits” (vv. 16–20). Some of the false prophets’ fruits are mentioned in the NT: controversies (1 Tim. 1:3); divisions (1 Tim. 6:3, 4); greed (6:5–10); destruction of faith (2 Tim. 2:18); and self-destruction by heresy (2 Pet. 2:1).

The doubling of a name is an address of intimacy (Gen. 22:11; 1 Sam. 3:10; 2 Sam. 18:33; Luke 22:31). It is not claims or feelings of intimacy with Jesus that matter, nor is it performing miraculous works in Jesus’ name, as even Judas Iscariot did (Matt. 10:1–4). What matters is sincere obedience to the Father’s will, flowing from faith. Genuine intimacy with the Father means knowing God and being known by God (1 Cor. 8:2, 3).

Storms in Palestine are infrequent but can be violent. Although the houses of the foolish and the wise may for a long time appear equally secure, when the storm comes the destruction of the foolish one’s house is total (Is. 28:14–18). So it is with the life of those who hear the words of Jesus but do not take appropriate action in response (cf. James 1:22–25).
This formula signals the close of each of the five main discourses in Matthew (11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1).

The scribes, like the later rabbis, teach by citing what previous teachers had said. Their authority is the tradition. Jesus teaches directly from Scripture with His own authority, confidently correcting what previous generations have said (5:21, 22, 27, 28, 31, 32, etc.).
The order of the miracles and events in these chapters differs from that found in Mark and Luke. Matthew probably arranges them by topic rather than chronology.

A variety of skin diseases are referred to by the Gk. word used here, not just leprosy (Hansen’s disease). Touching a leper makes one ceremonially unclean (cf. Lev. 15:7), but in this case, rather than Jesus’ becoming unclean, the leper is healed and becomes clean.

The command to the leper to be silent is to prevent miracle seekers from hindering Jesus’ main mission, which is to proclaim God’s kingdom, bringing comprehensive—spiritual as well as physical—cleansing (Mark 1:38, 45). By showing himself to the priest, the leper will fulfill the requirements of the law and be able to rejoin Jewish society (Lev. 14:1–32).

A Roman military officer in charge of approximately one hundred men. This centurion has an appreciation for Jesus’ authority that surpasses anything in Israel, an awareness of his own unworthiness, and faith that Jesus can overcome the difficulty of his unworthiness. Matthew, who often prefers a condensed style, does not mention the intermediaries who appear in the parallel account in Luke 7:1–10.

The faith of the Gentile centurion provides the occasion for the prediction that Israel will be hardened and the gospel will be extended to the Gentiles. The Great Commission (28:18–20) closes the gospel with Jesus’ charge to make disciples of all nations.

verse_quote: recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
note: A reference to the messianic banquet theme of Is. 25:6–9. Gentiles now appear in place of the natural sons. This theme recurs in the parable of the wicked tenants (21:33–44, esp. v. 43) and the banquet parable (22:1–14). Jesus’ prediction is an early example of the principle developed by Paul in Rom. 9:30–32: Israel tries to pursue righteousness by works and does not obtain it, but Gentiles who know they deserve only condemnation seek God’s mercy and obtain it.
These figures of speech represent the grief and despair of those who are everlastingly excluded from the kingdom.

Is. 53:4 mentions “griefs” and “sorrows” (rendered “illnesses” and “diseases” in Matthew) as resulting from sin, for which they are the curse (Is. 53:5). Jesus came to bear the curse as well as the guilt of sin on the cross, and in His ministry He demonstrated the power of His coming death and resurrection to reverse all the effects of Adam’s fall (including physical effects) for those who trust Him. Yet He has not promised to remove sickness from the world or the church before the second coming (Rom. 8:20–23; 1 Cor. 15:26), when our lowly bodies will be conformed to His glorious body through resurrection (Phil. 3:20, 21).

These two events show the radical commitment Jesus demands of disciples. Those who identify with Jesus will be “sojourners and exiles” in the world (1 Pet. 2:11). Honoring one’s parents by providing a proper burial was a strict obligation in Jewish society, a fitting application of the fifth commandment (Ex. 20:12), which Jesus affirmed as God’s Word (Matt. 15:4–6). But Jesus demands a greater allegiance to Himself.

This title occurs only three times in the NT outside the Gospels (Acts 7:56; Rev. 1:13; 14:14). All of the many occurrences in the Gospels involve assertions made by Jesus about Himself and may be classified into three categories. (1) “Son of Man” can mean “a human being,” especially in statements about what is typical of humanity generally. This use is similar to God’s calling Ezekiel “son of man” (Ezek. 2:1 note) or to Paul’s reference to the human race as “the sons of men” (Eph. 3:5). (2) The title is used by Jesus when He predicts the suffering, death, and resurrection He would accomplish for humanity (17:22, 23 note). (3) It can refer to the apocalyptic “Son of Man” who appears at the judgment at the end times (24:30; 26:64 note). This usage stems from Dan. 7:13, 14, where “one like a son of man” appears before the Ancient of Days and receives world dominion and worship. Jesus may have used “Son of Man” and avoided using “Messiah” because of popular conceptions that the Messiah would be a political and military leader. Yet in Dan. 7, the Ancient of Days confers on the one like a son of man “dominion ... that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him”—a prophecy now being fulfilled as the ascended Son of Man expands His reign through the global preaching of the gospel (Matt. 28:18–20).

Jesus’ sleeping may well be an allusion to David’s sleeping in Pss. 3 and 4. There, David’s sleeping indicates his trust as a king in God to deliver him from impending danger. David’s trust expressed in sleep points to Jesus, the greater Davidic king, who now is portrayed as the perfectly trusting king., 25

The psalmists answer the disciples’ astonished question, “What sort of man is this?” Only God can still turbulent and threatening seas as Lord of the storm (Pss. 29:3, 4; 65:5–7; 89:9; 107:23–30, the latter of which is likely alluded to here). Jesus is not only the perfect king who perfectly trusts in God but also God Himself incarnate.

**two demon-possessed men.** Perhaps only one of these two demoniacs is exceedingly violent, so Mark and Luke mention only that one. Matthew may mention both to suggest that two witnesses attest this victory of Jesus over demons (Deut. 19:15; see Matt. 18:16; 20:30).

See note on 16:16.

**the time.** The demons complain that it is not yet “the time,” the day of judgment. But Jesus is present and God’s kingdom is near, so the powers of darkness cannot resist the king’s liberating light (12:28).

The Gk. word translated “demons” is a broad term for “divinities” (Acts 17:18), that is, supernatural beings. “Unclean spirits” (10:1) cause havoc with men, sometimes by possession. They are in league with Satan, the prince of demons (9:34; 12:24–28).

The demons ask permission to enter a herd of pigs, apparently imagining that this will prolong their influence on earth. But their defiling presence drives the disturbed swine into the sea, hastening the spirits’ consignment to the abyss (Luke 8:31). Subsequent events demonstrate the perverse values of the people, who prefer their pigs to the rescue of two human beings.
Forgiveness is the prerogative of the one who has been offended, so for Jesus to forgive sins is to claim divine authority (Is. 43:25), as the scribes rightly discern.

Ultimately, forgiving sins is more difficult than performing a miracle, as the scribes understand, since they recognize that only God can forgive sins. But the forgiveness of sins cannot be seen by observers. Jesus performs the lesser deed to prove the greater, showing that He has authority as Son of Man to render a justifying verdict not only in heaven after His exaltation (Dan. 7:13, 14) but also presently on earth.

Just as Jesus is not defiled by contact with lepers, so He is not defiled by contact with sinners such as Matthew and his colleagues who collaborate with Rome’s occupying forces. He is the physician who heals spiritual as well as physical sickness. Those who think they are well are puzzled by Jesus’ activities and found Him offensive.

Although Luke notes that Pharisees ask about fasting, Mark includes both John’s disciples and Pharisees among those who raise the question. John’s summons to sorrow over sin in view of the coming kingdom make the self-denial of fasting an appropriate practice for his disciples (Lev. 16:29–31; Ps. 35:13).

John characterized Jesus as the bridegroom to whom the bride belongs (John 3:29, 30), evoking OT imagery of Israel as the Lord’s bride (Jer. 2:2, 3; Hos. 2:2–20). The arrival of the groom brings the joy of the wedding feast, at which fasting is not fitting.

**then they will fast.** Jesus recognizes a future time when the bridegroom will not be with them. This points out that from the earliest stages of His ministry, Jesus has anticipated a time between His initial coming in redemption and His final coming to consummate both judgment and salvation.

verse_quote: new wine put into old wineskins.
note: New wine continues to ferment and builds up pressure that will burst a used wineskin. Old patterns of piety are inappropriate while the king is present, although Jesus assumes that His followers may resume fasting after His ascension if they do so out of proper motives (6:16–18).

As usual, Matthew has a more condensed form of this story than Mark and Luke. The stories of the ruler’s daughter and of the woman with a hemorrhage, whom Jesus calls “daughter,” illustrate the relation between the work of Jesus and the role of faith in the kingdom. The same point appears in the following accounts of the blind man and the mute demoniac. These works (raising the dead, healing the sick, etc.) are in response to faith.

verse_quote: your faith has made you well.
note: Her faith has made her well because the blessings of the kingdom come to those who look to Jesus for the solution to their problems, not because of any power of faith in itself.
Professional mourners and others who help the bereaved express their grief.
Jesus is prophesying that He will raise her from death (John 11:11–14; 1 Thess. 4:13–18). In the presence of the Lord of life, death is no more final or irreversible than slumber.

This healing of two blind men is similar to the account in 20:29–34, which seems to be parallel to the healing of Bartimaeus in Mark 10:46–52 (cf. Luke 18:35–43). Both Bartimaeus and the blind men in Matt. 9 and 20 express their faith by calling Jesus “Son of David,” a messianic title. The similarities have suggested to some that both accounts in Matthew are based on the healing of Bartimaeus, but differences between the two accounts in Matthew suggest separate incidents.

This paragraph summarizes the activity of Jesus in chs. 5–9 (teaching, preaching, healing; cf. 4:23) and introduces the mission discourse of ch. 10. The background is Ezek. 34:5, 6. Jesus is the true Shepherd, who is concerned for His sheep (John 10), and He is identified with the “Lord God” of Ezek. 34:11–16.

Often a metaphor for the end-time activity of God. That the harvest is plentiful indicates that the harvest is not the harvest time (as in John 4:35) but the crop (as in Luke 10:2). The emphasis here is on the proclamation of the gospel, the eschatological announcement that precedes judgment and urges people to repent and believe God’s promises. The “laborers” are not the angels sent to gather for judgment (13:49) but disciples who imitate Jesus by proclaiming the coming of the kingdom (10:7). Jesus first commands His disciples to pray to God to send workers, and then He immediately sends these same men out to announce the near approach of God’s kingdom and to exert its power over evil.

The Gk. word _apostolos_ designates an authorized representative or emissary whose word has the authority of the sender (cf. 2 Cor. 8:23, where it is translated “messengers,” and 2 Cor. 1:1 note). Here the Twelve receive authority to do exactly what Jesus has been doing (vv. 7, 8).

A member of a revolutionary movement (“Simon ... called the Zealot,” Luke 6:15). According to Josephus, the Zealots were a political party whose religious enthusiasm led them to advocate armed rebellion against Rome. Simon’s presence among the Twelve, along with Matthew, a tax collector who collaborated with Roman functionaries, shows the reconciling power of Christ.

**Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.** Well before the turning point where Jesus speaks explicitly of His coming suffering (16:21), the cross casts its shadow over His inner circle. As He sends these apostles out, He now prepares them for persecution, even to the extreme of the cross, (10:38) like the one awaiting their master (10:24, 25).

This section contains several lines of teaching regarding the Christian mission that are found elsewhere in the other Gospels. This does not mean Matthew invented the occasion for the teaching, but in this, the second of the five major discourses, he may include relevant materi­al taught by Jesus on other occasions. Particularly 10:17–22, which envisions a world mission and being “dragged before governors and kings” (v. 18), seems to go beyond v. 5, which restricts the mission to Israel. Nevertheless, the future mission of the disciples to the whole world (28:18–20) is linked to this early experience of preaching to Israel, and Matthew’s grouping of the material is appropriate.

**10:5 Go nowhere among the Gentiles.** Although Jesus has already commended a Gentile’s faith as greater than that found in Israel (8:10), the focus of this first mission of the disciples, like that of Jesus generally before His passion and resurrection (15:24), is to the biological descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Israel’s “lost sheep” (Ezek. 34:16). Faithful to His promises to the patriarchs, God has sent His Messiah to bring salvation “to the Jew first, and also to the Greek” (Rom. 1:16).

The same signs of the kingdom that Jesus performed in chs. 8; 9 will be done by His disciples.

**10:8 give without pay.** The kingdom was given to the disciples freely; to peddle the message would insult God and obscure the nature of the gospel as a free gift. Nevertheless, they will be sustained; they do not need extra travel money and provisions (vv. 9, 10). Paul later refuses financial support from those whom he is the first to evangelize, while accepting support from established churches and directing them to provide for their teachers (1 Cor. 9:12–18; Phil. 4:14–19; Gal. 6:6).

verse_quote: shake off the dust from your feet.
note: That is, the dust on one’s garment kicked up by the feet. Jews sometimes shook the dust off their clothing when returning from Gentile lands as a sign of contempt; Jesus uses it here as a sign of judgment. A town that does not receive Jesus’ representatives does not receive Jesus and becomes spiritually defiled and is subject to judgment as Sodom and Gomorrah (Acts 13:51).

These verses anticipate a later, more extensive mission than the immediate occasion of v. 5 (10:5–11:1 note). Persecution will occur at the hands of both Jewish (v. 17) and Gentile (v. 18) authorities. But disciples are not to respond to this as pagans do, by hiring professional orators to defend them in court. The Holy Spirit will provide their defense (Acts 4:8).
Every kind of people. The allusion is to Mic. 7:6, which Jesus later quotes (v. 35).

verse_quote: before the Son of Man comes.
note: There are several interpretations of this coming of the Son of Man: (1) The coming is the second coming of Christ to judge the earth. This view fits most of the other occurrences of the phrase (24:30; 25:31; 26:64; but see 16:28). The chief difficulty is that the note of urgency in v. 23 seems incompatible with a delay until the last judgment. (2) The coming is the resurrection and ascension of Jesus or the sending of the Spirit at Pentecost. However, there is no evidence that the disciples were persecuted with the intensity assumed in vv. 17–22 before Jesus’ resurrection or Pentecost. (3) The phrase “before the Son of Man comes” is a way of saying, “before I rejoin you.” But again, the persecution described in vv. 17–22 does not occur during this time, and the purpose for the coming of the Son of Man elsewhere (to bring judgment) makes this meaning unlikely. (4) The coming refers to the destruction of Jerusalem in A.D. 70 as an act of judgment against the nation of Israel. Although the NT writers do not typically use this word for the destruction of Jerusalem, this understanding retains the note of urgency and fits the experience of the church before A.D. 70. It may be the traumatic time that Jesus foretells when He says that the Jewish leaders will “see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of power” (which begins at His ascension) “and coming on the clouds of heaven” in providential judgment through Rome’s legions (Matt. 26:64). Other references to the coming of the Son of Man present it as a terrible display of God’s judgment. Although these cannot be limited to the destruction of Jerusalem, that event was terrible in intensity and fell on what had been the central visible symbol of God’s presence, the temple.

Gk. _beelzeboul_, a transliteration of a Hb. or Aramaic name for the prince of demons, through whose cooperation Jesus allegedly exorcises unclean spirits according to His critics among the Pharisees (12:24–27). The name probably means “lord of heaven” and appears in the OT in the intentionally distorted form Baal-zebub (“lord of the flies”) as a name for the god of Ekron (2 Kin. 1:2).

This injunction to fear God and not people is perhaps a development of Is. 8:12, 13 (cf. 1 Pet. 3:14, 15). It is supported by four arguments: (1) the acts of the wicked will be exposed for what they are; (2) although people can kill the body, God can punish soul and body; (3) God orders everything, down to the fall of a sparrow and the number of hairs on the head; and (4) those who deny Jesus when threatened by humans will be denied by Jesus in the presence of His heavenly Father. The Bible consistently teaches that fear and reverence are appropriate responses to God.
See note on 5:22.

Mic. 7:6 addresses the rebelliousness and strife characteristic of Israel during the time of Ahaz. Just as Israel’s history foreshadows Jesus’ history (2:15 note), its turmoil and strife foreshadow the strife that results from the coming of the Messiah (Luke 2:34, 35), even to the division of families. Although coming to Christ brings peace to the heart (11:29) and even reconciliation between generations (Luke 1:17), embracing the gospel also makes life more difficult in some respects, for Jesus demands allegiance that takes priority over the natural ties of life (Matt. 10:37–39).
This is to obey and identify with Jesus even unto death, not simply to bear some particular burden imposed by the Lord.
This verse emphasizes the principle that receiving those who are emissaries of another is equivalent to receiving the person who sent them (v. 40).

While not excluding children, this phrase refers to all Jesus’ disciples, who are like little children, vulnerable and unable to repay kindnesses shown them by others (18:1–6, 10, 14). Jesus so identifies Himself with these “little ones” that mercy shown to them will be rewarded as mercy shown to the King Himself (25:31–46).

John the Baptist predicted that the coming one would bring judgment, chopping down the trees of wickedness (3:10, 12). Presumably John heard reports of Jesus’ exorcisms and miraculous healings, which show that He is the Messiah. But Jesus allows His forerunner to be imprisoned by the wicked Herod, evoking John’s question whether He is indeed the royal executor of divine justice for which God’s suffering people have been longing.

Jesus invites John’s disciples to witness His miracles, which directly fulfill Is. 35:5, 6. Jesus the Messiah will one day inflict on the wicked the judgment they deserve, but in His first coming His purpose is to bring blessing by bearing God’s judgment on others’ behalf.

John the Baptist is the immediate forerunner of the One to whom all the prophets pointed, and hence he points to Christ more clearly than they did. As such, he himself is the object of prophecy, the one predicted in Mal. 3:1, the fulfillment of the Elijah prophecy of Mal. 4:5, 6 (Matt. 11:14), the herald of the Lord’s arrival (3:3; cf. Is. 40:3).

The least in the kingdom are more privileged than John because they stand after the cross and resurrection and thus, having received the fullness of the Spirit and the revelation of Christ’s full ministry in the new age, they participate in what the prophets only saw from a distance (1 Pet. 1:10–12). Thus, the “least in the kingdom of heaven” is greater than John because they have received more revelation than any OT prophet, including John, the greatest prophet of the old age.

The kingdom is pressing ahead with force, although violent men such as Herod are trying to overcome it by force. It is not the strong and forceful who obtain the kingdom but the weak and helpless who depend on God (vv. 28–30; cf. Luke 16:16 note).

Jesus identifies John the Baptist as the Elijah who Malachi predicted would come as the forerunner of the Messiah (Mal. 4:5). Believing this identification requires the eyes of faith (“if you are willing to accept it”). There may have been some misunderstanding in the first century that Elijah himself would return to earth, but John denied that he was Elijah in that sense (John 1:21). The angel Gabriel’s announcement was that John would come “in the spirit and power” of Elijah (Luke 1:17).

People who resist God’s Word can always find an excuse by critiquing God’s messengers. Like children stubbornly complaining that others do not dance to their tune, “this generation” critiques John for his austerity and conscience-indicting call to repentance and then turns around and complains that Jesus’ style is too celebratory and welcoming of unseemly, undeserving companions.

See note on 8:20.

**wisdom is justified by her deeds.** Despite the contrast in the tones of their ministries, both John and Jesus bring God’s wisdom, as is demonstrated by the redemptive outcome of their deeds.

verse_quote: the cities where most of his mighty works had been done.
note: King Ahab’s alliance by marriage with Sidon led to the rampant spread of Baal worship in Israel (1 Kin. 16:31–33), and both Tyre and Sidon were condemned by God’s prophets (Is. 23; Ezek. 27; 28). God’s destruction of Sodom by fire for its perversion and injustice (Gen. 19) turned the city into a byword exemplifying the ruinous results of sin. The Galilean towns that have witnessed Jesus’ miracles may not have sunk to the same depth of degradation, but exposure to the fuller revelation of the Messiah makes them more culpable than those pagan cities. See Luke 12:48.
God is sovereign in choosing those to whom He will reveal His truth. No one can know God by worldly wisdom and learning (1 Cor. 1:26–31).

Jesus makes extraordinary claims. He claims that God’s sovereign disposition of all things has been committed to Him. As in Dan. 7, the Son of Man has received all power and dominion (anticipating Matt. 28:18). He alone knows the Father and can reveal the Father to others (John 14:6). The Father alone knows Him, so Peter’s later confession that Jesus is the Christ can only be through the Father’s revelation of the Son (Matt. 16:16, 17). Jesus’ knowledge is equal to the Father’s, and His sonship is unique.

Echoing personified wisdom in Prov. 9:1–5 and intertestamental wisdom literature, Jesus invites the weary to find rest and refreshment in Him. He does not extend His invitation to those who are naturally intelligent but to little children (v. 25), not to the strong but to the weary and heavy-laden. Both Jesus and John convey God’s wisdom (v. 19 note), but Jesus transcends His forerunner, for He Himself is the incarnate wisdom of God.

verse_quote: Take my yoke ... my yoke is easy.
note: The yoke, placed on the shoulders of beasts and humans who pull plows and wagons, symbolizes submission and slavery (Gen. 27:40; Is. 10:27; Hos. 11:4). Jewish sources spoke of the yoke of the law and of wisdom. Though the law was God’s good gift to His people, the scribes’ oral traditions and the spiritual disability of sinful humanity turned the law into an unbearable burden (12:2 note; 15:2; 23:2–4; Acts 15:10). When the law was understood as a way of meriting salvation, it became a “yoke of slavery” (Gal. 5:1). By contrast, the yoke of Jesus, while demanding, is “easy” because it is from one who is “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matt. 11:29, 30). He has fulfilled the law’s righteous demand perfectly for His people (Matt. 3:15; Gal. 4:4, 5; 2 Cor. 5:21), and His Spirit empowers their grateful obedience (Rom. 8:2–4). Therefore, He alone can provide true rest for the soul., 30

God’s law requires farmers to leave grain at the edge of fields to be gleaned by those in need (Lev. 19:9, 10; Deut. 23:24, 25), and it does not prohibit plucking grain on the Sabbath in order to satisfy hunger—after all, the disciples are not farmers laboring in the harvest. The Pharisees’ objections are based on an oral tradition that both obscures and counters the law’s true purpose.

**Sabbath.** The Sabbath is a symbol of God’s sovereignty over the whole created universe (Ex. 20:8). It is a reminder of His redemption of His people (Deut. 5:12), and it is a representation of the hope of eternal rest at the consummation (Heb. 4:9). As Lord of the Sabbath, Jesus fulfills all aspects of the meaning of the Sabbath (Col. 2:16, 17), and He defines how His followers should observe the Sabbath. Regulations that contravene the Sabbath’s life-sustaining and life-restoring purposes are at cross-purposes with God’s design for the day (Matt. 12:9–13).

In His reply to the accusations of the Pharisees, Jesus uses two arguments from the lesser to the greater, both focusing on His own person and authority. In an hour of need, David, God’s anointed, transgressed a ceremonial law concerning the bread of the presence in the tabernacle. Now one with much greater authority is present. Similarly, the demands of temple worship require priests to labor on the Sabbath, and now “something greater than the temple” is here (v. 6).

The one in whom God dwells personally is greater than God’s dwelling place in Israel that foreshadowed the incarnate Son. Jesus, Immanuel (“God with us”), is the true temple to whom the symbol pointed (John 1:14; 2:21). The disciples, being in the presence of Jesus, have a far greater service than the priests who served in the Jerusalem temple. Jesus is greater not only than the temple (associated with priests) but also than ancient prophets such as Jonah (Matt. 12:41) and the great sage-king Solomon (12:42).

Again quoting Hos. 6:6 (cf. 9:13), Jesus condemns the Pharisees’ perversion of the Sabbath, multiplying regulatory restrictions and minimizing God’s merciful purpose for granting His people rest (Matt. 11:29; cf. Mark 2:27).

The Son of Man has received dominion over creation (8:20 note) and redemption (20:28). So also He has dominion over the Sabbath, the sign of God’s sovereignty in creation and redemption (v. 2 note). The claims Jesus makes here (as well as His disregard of rabbinic tradition in His practice) undoubtedly shock the Pharisees, furthering their resolve to kill Him (v. 14).

Another example of Christ’s lordship over the Sabbath. Again, no OT text prohibits healing on the Sabbath, and Jesus’ critics’ practice of rescuing an at-risk sheep in an emergency reinforces Jesus’ logic that the Sabbath is a fitting day to heal human beings, who bear God’s image and exceed sheep in value. Jesus does not teach that the Sabbath is abolished by the coming of the kingdom. He has come not to destroy the law but to fulfill it (5:17 note). The problem is not that the Pharisees observe the Sabbath but that they misinterpret it and turn what should be a delight into a burden.

verse_quote: ordered them not to make him known.
note: Is. 42:1–4 is cited as an explanation of why Jesus commands people not to reveal to others who He is. He has come to proclaim and establish justice, but not by a showy display of power and not by leading a political or military movement (11:4–6 note). The Messiah, who is gentle and lowly in heart (11:29), will enter Jerusalem in humility (21:5) and defeat His and our great enemy through humbly enduring crucifixion (1 Cor. 1:18; Col. 2:14, 15).
See note on 10:25.
Jesus’ deity is manifest in His knowledge of people’s thoughts, regardless of whether they articulate them aloud or in His hearing (9:4; John 2:24, 25).

By His victory over Satan in the wilderness (3:16, 4:1; 4:10 note) and exorcism of demons, Jesus demonstrates that He has bound the “strong man” and that Satan is powerless to prevent the coming of the kingdom. The binding of Satan is a symbol of the messianic age in Jewish apocalyptic literature (see also Rev. 20:2).

To call the work of God’s Spirit the work of Satan involves an explicit, willful, and decisive rejection of the very divine person who alone can bring about repentance. The notion of the “unforgivable sin” has caused needless anxiety. Anyone who has been convicted of sin by the Spirit (John 16:8) and now believes the truth cannot possibly have committed it. See theological note “The Unforgivable Sin” on p. 1739. One result of the divine Son’s humility in His incarnation is that ignorant slander against Him can be forgiven when the Spirit grants repentance (1 Tim. 1:13–16)., 32
Through the metaphors of trees and treasures, Jesus teaches that the words one speaks reveal the condition of one’s heart, whether good and healthy or bad and diseased (see 15:10–20).

Words, even carelessly spoken words, are eternally important. Scripture condemns verbal sins such as lies, gossip, or insults as severely as it condemns adultery and murder (5:22, 37; 2 Cor. 12:20; 1 Tim. 1:10; James 3:6; Rev. 21:8)., 37

That they should ask for a sign is incredible in the light of what they have already seen, which provoked their conspiracy against Jesus (12:14). Jesus does not do miracles on demand. Yet God will give one climactic sign, the resurrection of His Son from the dead, and that sign will expose the adamant rebellion of that unbelieving generation.

Jonah was swept away from the land of the living in the sea and the great fish but then restored to life again to proclaim God’s word to Nineveh. The Son of Man’s rising from the dead (v. 40) is the greatest sign of all that the kingdom has come. The repentance of the notorious Gentiles of Nineveh shames Israel’s hardness of heart when confronted with one greater than Jonah.
An emphatic way of saying “three days.”
The lengths traveled by a Gentile queen to hear Solomon’s wisdom again indicts those who doubt and resist Christ, who is wisdom incarnate.

The dispute over Jesus’ power to exorcise demons (12:22–32) leads Him to use exorcism as an illustration to show that ridding oneself of evil influences only creates a dangerous spiritual vacuum. Unless God’s Spirit takes up residence (Rom. 8:9), a person purged by self-denial becomes vulnerable to reinfestation by graver evils such as pride, hypocrisy, and contempt for others.
This collection of parables on the nature of the kingdom of heaven is the third great discourse in Matthew (Introduction: Literary Features).

The term “parable,” like the OT term translated “proverb,” refers broadly to a comparison of some sort. Jesus’ parables are His distinctive teaching through brief comparisons or longer narratives. They usually have one central point, although some have multiple points of correspondence between elements in the story and the realities they symbolize; e.g., four soils referring to four types of hearers (13:18–23) or two sons symbolizing flagrant sinners and the judgmental self-righteous (Luke 15:1, 2, 11–32; cf. Matt. 21:28–32). Most of Jesus’ parables are clear, but they also contain a depth of meaning that only one with a right relationship to Jesus can comprehend. It is only to the disciples that Jesus gives the interpretation of the parable of the sower (vv. 18–23) and the parable of the weeds (vv. 36–43). The ungodly miss this deeper meaning because their lack of a proper relationship with God has darkened their thoughts and hearts (Rom. 1:21).

**A sower.** Contrary to expectations that the inbreaking of God’s kingdom would be a harvest season, when the righteous are gathered and the wicked destroyed (Ps. 1:3–5), Jesus’ first coming is a season of sowing, in which the word that He disseminates, like vulnerable seed, meets both resistant and receptive responses.

The ability to understand God’s message, let alone respond to it, is the gift of God, distributed according to His sovereign choice.

**13:11 To you ... to them.** “Secrets” may be better translated “mysteries,” as an allusion to Dan. 2:28–30, 47, where God reveals to the unbelieving Babylonian king a parabolic prophetic vision, which must be interpreted for him by Daniel. The focus of the vision is on God’s future defeat of the kingdoms of evil and the establishment of His kingdom on earth. Jesus sees this as beginning to be fulfilled in His ministry, albeit mysteriously. The “mystery” is that Daniel’s kingdom is beginning to be fulfilled but in an unexpected way. The following parables reveal that it starts small and will only slowly and invisibly reach great size. The kingdom is present, but there is no final judgment or reward, and both the wicked and righteous still exist together. These are unexpected features of the kingdom from the Jewish perspective, which anticipates a great kingdom that will come suddenly in full form and where the wicked will be judged and the righteous rewarded. See theological note “The Illumination of the Holy Spirit” on p. 2018.

To those who have a relationship with Jesus, parables deepen understanding and foster that relationship, but to those who do not, parables increase their confusion and ignorance. Thus the function of parables is both to enlighten and to conceal.

Mark 4:12 (cf. Luke 8:10) phrases this statement even more strongly, with “so that” rather than “because.” For Mark, Jesus’ purpose in telling parables is to prevent understanding and to cause unbelief (Mark 4:11 note); in Matthew, Jesus’ parables are in response to people’s unbelief and inability to understand. Though some see Matthew as softening the divine sovereignty emphasized in Mark, the word “lest” in v. 15 indicates that God’s sovereign choice lies behind the hardening of hearts, deafening of ears, and blinding of eyes. While Matthew highlights the culpability of those who reject Christ, his citation of Is. 6:9, 10 illustrates the compatibility of God’s sovereignty and human responsibility. The parables serve as an instrument of judgment by hardening the impenitent.

Jesus’ disciples and NT believers are doubly blessed. God’s grace has made their hearts, ears, and eyes receptive to the revelation of His kingdom; and they live in the era of the fulfillment of God’s promises, for which OT believers earnestly hoped., 17
See theological note “The Kingdom of God” on p. 1823.

Two soils represent initially positive responses to the word that prove fruitless in the end. Rocky soil symbolizes an immediate interest—“with joy”—that proves shallow and withers in the face of persecution. Thorny soil shows the danger of distraction by means of the worries and pleasures of everyday life. Again, what seems at first to be a positive response to the word yields no final harvest.
Wealth is a blessing from God if He is honored, but it is a dangerous snare if it captivates the heart (Eccl. 5:19; 1 Tim. 6:9).

verse_quote: who hears the word and understands it.
note: Only hearing and understanding the word (a faith that finds expression in obedience is implied) results in fruit. Some temporarily receive the word but fall away to avoid opposition or to pursue earthly wealth (v. 22). Likewise there are differing levels of bearing fruit. There are ultimately only two kinds of ground, that which “holds fast” the word and bears fruit “with patience” (Luke 8:15), and that which does not.

Again, Jesus Himself provides the interpretation (vv. 36–43). The field is the whole world, not just Israel or the church. God withholds immediate judgment for the sake of the elect who are in the world. The righteous have had to live in the midst of the unrighteous from the beginning.

The mustard shrub can grow to a height of ten feet (3 m). The inbreaking of God’s kingdom seems insignificant, almost imperceptible, like a tiny seed or like yeast hidden in bread dough, yet its influence will eventually spread throughout the nations. Certainly in the first century, the kingdom of heaven appears to be nothing in comparison with Rome, yet it will prove to be much greater.
The picture of a tree with birds nesting in the branches recalls Ezek. 17:23, where the birds represent the Gentile nations taking refuge in the Messiah and enjoying the blessings of the covenant.
Although leaven or yeast is often a symbol of evil (16:11), here the analogy makes a positive point: the kingdom’s quiet presence will fill and change the world.

As the apex of Israel’s wisdom tradition, Jesus fulfills Ps. 78:2, where the “parables” or “dark sayings” are events in the history of God’s redemption of His people, climaxing in the choice of David as king. The redemptive events themselves are not “hidden,” but their meaning becomes clear only as the psalmist reveals their meaning. The psalm contains repeated patterns of Israel’s unbelief in the OT, which foreshadow the unbelieving patterns being recapitulated by Israel in not responding in faith to Jesus’ ministry., 35
See note on 8:20.

verse_quote: gather out ... all causes of sin.
note: The final judgment will be a separation not only of the ungodly from the godly but also of ungodliness from the godly. Note that the Son of Man will send _His_ angels—Jesus clearly asserts divine authority.
See theological note “Hell” on p. 1753.
An allusion to the promise of the future resurrection (Dan. 12:3).

Jesus’ parables display the heretofore hidden kingdom of heaven (v. 35), but its worth remains hidden from most people. Those who discover its priceless value, however, like a man who finds treasure in a field or the trader in pearls, gladly sacrifice anything and everything to obtain it (Phil. 3:8)., 45

As in the parable of the weeds, in this parable Jesus teaches that the separation of those who belong to the kingdom of heaven and those destined for destruction awaits the close of the age. Until that time, believers and unbelievers coexist as God’s reign advances quietly and invincibly.

Many scribes in Judaism are castigated by Jesus, not because of their positions as teachers but because, in their hypocrisy, their actions contradict their instruction. Yet the Gospels show us scribes who become Jesus’ disciples, such as Nicodemus (John 3:1, 10; 19:38–40), or who at least draw near to the kingdom (Mark 12:34).

**trained for the kingdom.** The Gk. phrase could be rendered “has become a disciple of the kingdom.” Since this saying immediately follows Jesus’ asking the disciples if they understand, the implication is that the disciples will become teachers and will, like a hospitable host, bring from their treasury to share with others the gifts they have received—an understanding both of Israel’s ancient redemptive history that anticipated Christ and of His fulfillment in new redemptive acts, which signal the presence of the kingdom.

As when Jesus read Is. 61 and declared it fulfilled in the synagogue of Nazareth (Luke 4:16–30), the neighbors among whom Jesus grew up found His teaching authority both amazing and offensive. Superficial acquaintance with God’s humble Messiah blinds His lifelong neighbors to His true identity (cf. John 4:44).
The Gk. word translated “carpenter” is also a general term for any craftsman or worker. Joseph could have worked with wood or stone.
Jesus’ refusal to do many miracles in Nazareth is not because He depended on the faith of people to empower Him but because those without faith will not grasp the miracle’s message (cf. 1 Cor. 13:2).

See notes on Mark 6:14, 17. Herod Antipas governed Galilee and Perea, roughly one-quarter of the realm once ruled by his late father, Herod the Great. Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea, would send Jesus (a Galilean) to Herod Antipas for a ruling on the Sanhedrin’s accusations. When Jesus would not perform to suit Herod’s curiosity, however, Herod returned Him without a verdict to Pilate (Luke 23:6–12).

A daughter by an earlier marriage to Herod Philip. According to the Jewish historian Josephus, the daughter’s name was Salome, and she later married another son of Herod the Great, Philip the tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis (Luke 3:1).

verse_quote: his disciples came and took the body.
note: John’s disciples thus honor the prophet who brought God’s word to them; and Joseph of Arimathea will similarly express a disciple’s devotion by claiming Jesus’ body and arranging His burial after the apostles themselves abandon Him in fear (27:57–60).

According to v. 2, enough time has elapsed after the death of John the Baptist for reports of Jesus’ miracles to come back to Herod, leading the tetrarch to fear that God has raised his prophetic accuser from the dead. Jesus hears about Herod’s renewed inquiries and crosses the Sea of Galilee to its northeastern shore, far from Tiberias, Herod’s capital.

The feeding of the five thousand is one of the few miracles, besides Jesus’ resurrection, that is recorded in all four Gospels (Mark 6:32–44; Luke 9:10–17; John 6:1–15). As God provided manna for Israel in the wilderness in the days of Moses, so Jesus provides bread for the people in a remote place. Matthew reports the details concisely, whereas John elaborates at length the significance of the miracle as a sign that Jesus is the bread of life, given from heaven.

Jesus challenges the disciples to provide for the crowd. Then, when they confess how inadequate their resources are, He blesses His heavenly Father, multiplies the small loaves and fish, and enlists His disciples to be ministers of His provision.
The hours before dawn, between three and six a.m.

OT echoes signal that Jesus is the Lord who rules the unruly sea, who “trampled the waves of the sea” (Job 9:8; Ps. 77:19; Is. 43:16).

**14:27 it is I.** The Gk. phrase (lit. “I am”) may allude to the Septuagint’s rendering of the divine name “I am,” revealed to Moses (Ex. 3:14).
The danger that a psalmist described metaphorically, Peter experiences literally, crying out to the divine Lord who alone can save him (Ps. 69:1–3).

verse_quote: the wind ceased ... Son of God.
note: Jesus again stills a storm (see 8:23–27), showing Himself to be the Lord of all creation, the One who rescues those who cry out to Him in distress (Ps. 107:23–32). This time His disciples have advanced from astonished confusion about His identity to confession that He is the Son of God, a title that expresses His messiahship and His deity, anticipating Peter’s landmark confession near Caesarea Philippi (16:16).,

The law of Moses requires washing for cleansing from various types of ceremonial defilement, especially of priests serving at the sanctuary (Ex. 30:18–21; Lev. 22:4–7). But it does not demand washing before every meal. The Pharisees regard the oral law, conveyed as tradition by the elders, as having equal authority with the written law. This tradition was later compiled as the _Mishnah_ in the second century. One of its treatises covers details of hand washing.

The fifth commandment entails not only a respectful attitude but also tangible support when they have need. To evade this responsibility by designating a gift to be paid (eventually) to the temple is to exalt a human tradition over God’s command in Scripture itself. Cherished traditional understandings must not supplant or obscure the Bible itself, nor should customs be elevated to the level of divine law. See theological note “Legalism” on p. 1713.

Apparently the disciples give too much weight to the opinion of the Pharisees; but Jesus has no need to please those whose claim to authority is not “planted” by God and who presume to guide others, though they themselves lack spiritual sight.

verse_quote: what comes out of the mouth.
note: The words that proceed from one’s mouth reveal the state of one’s heart, the corruption that renders one defiled in the sight of God (12:36, 37 note).

In judgment on ancient Israel, God removed His word, in the person of the prophet Elijah, to this region to bring blessing to a widow and her son in Zarephath (1 Kin. 17:9). So now Jesus withdraws from Galilee and brings blessing to a non-Israelite, a Canaanite, in this pagan territory.

verse_quote: only to the lost sheep ... of Israel.
note: Before the resurrection, the “wall” dividing Israel from the Gentile nations (Eph. 2:14) still stood; and Jesus sent the Twelve to Israel’s lost sheep (Matt. 10:5, 6).
