Jesus came as the Messiah and heir to the throne of David to fulfill God’s promises to the patriarchs (Rom. 15:8). Yet Jesus graciously responds to this Gentile woman’s humility, lack of presumption, and unreserved confidence that His mercy and power are more than sufficient to overflow boundaries of the covenant community and to supply her daughter’s desperate need.

Jesus’ term can refer to house pets rather than strays on the street, and the woman extends the imagery by portraying the dogs as awaiting scraps while the children dine. Nonetheless, the association of dogs with uncleanness (Matt. 7:6; 1 Sam. 17:43), and therefore with Gentiles, lies behind Jesus’ metaphor. He reminds the petitioner of her status in relation to Israel’s God, and she concurs with humility yet with hope.

Mark indicates that these events take place in the Decapolis (Mark 7:31), a predominantly Gentile area, as may be implied by Matthew’s “they glorified the God of Israel” (Matt 15:31). Since it follows the story of the Canaanite woman near Tyre and Sidon, this account of Jesus’ healings, exorcisms, and feeding of four thousand men, “besides women and children,” offers more evidence that His grace overflows in blessing beyond the confines of Israel’s lost sheep. Here is the Gentile counterpart of the feeding of five thousand in Galilee (presumably Jews), a sign that the son and seed of Abraham brings blessing to all nations (1:1; 28:19, 20; Gal. 3:16).

The demand for a sign “from heaven” expresses a stubborn refusal to acknowledge the heavenly source of the many miracles that Jesus has performed. Jesus notes the irony that the Pharisees and Sadducees can interpret the heavens—that is, the sky—to predict weather but fail to grasp what His miracles signify about the spiritual weather, that is, the times in which they live, the era of the Messiah’s coming. The problem is not lack of evidence but an unwillingness to accept its significance.

As in 12:38–41, Jesus again cites the prophet Jonah’s “resurrection” from entombment in the sea and the great fish as a preview of His own resurrection from death itself, which is the greatest sign of His messiahship.

Before commemorating the exodus in the annual celebration of Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, Jews are to remove from their homes all baked goods containing yeast (Ex. 12:15–19). Thus, yeast (leaven) often symbolizes that which defiles (Lev. 2:11; 6:17), as it does here (but see Matt. 13:33)

Jesus frequently speaks in parables, but His disciples here think He is speaking literally (v. 7). They should realize from His feeding miracles that Jesus can provide food when needed and so recognize that He is symbolizing the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees as insidiously defiling. False teaching, like leaven in dough, can permeate a church and corrupt its faith and holiness (1 Cor. 5:6–8; Gal. 5:9)., 12

A predominantly pagan city near Mount Hermon, about twenty-five miles (40 km) north of Galilee. Over the course of its history, Caesarea Philippi was a center of worship to the Canaanite god Baal, of the Gk. god Pan, and of Augustus, the first Roman emperor.

verse_quote: John the Baptist ... Elijah ... Jeremiah or one of the prophets.
note: Jesus also has been identified as an ally of Beelzebul/Satan (12:24–26), but His disciples report only the complimentary opinions circulating among those who have heard His words and seen His deeds.

verse_quote: who do you say that I am.
note: The “you” is plural. Peter answers on behalf of the Twelve, and his confession of Jesus’ identity sets the church apart from those outside its community, even those who admire Him from a distance.

Peter declares that Jesus is the Messiah and king prophesied in the OT (1:1 note).

**the Son of the living God.** The meaning of the title “Son of God” is different from that of pagan literature. In the OT, the anointed king is called a “son” of God (2 Sam. 7:14; Ps. 2:7). Israel as a whole is also God’s “son” (Ex. 4:22), and Jesus fulfills this status of Israel (2:15 note). As applied to Jesus, the title reflects Jesus’ unique relation to the Father (11:27; 21:38). He is acknowledged by the Father as “my beloved Son” (3:17; 17:5). The triunity of the one true God is implied in the Great Commission that closes this gospel, as the apostles are told to baptize disciples “in the [singular] name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (28:19).

Peter’s understanding has been given to him from above, going beyond what he can discern on his own. Just as only the Son can reveal the Father (11:27), so only the Father can enable anyone to recognize the Son’s true identity. See Jonathan Edwards's sermon on this text, "A Divine and Supernatural Light."

The name “Peter” (_Petros_), which is also one of the Gk. words for “rock,” is a play on another Gk. word for “rock” (_petra_). There are four leading interpretations of this play on words: (1) Peter’s confession that Jesus is “the Christ” (v. 16) is the rock upon which the church is built; (2) Jesus Himself is the rock, as Peter later testifies (1 Pet. 2:5–8); (3) Peter, as the representative apostle, is a foundation in the church, (Eph. 2:20); (4) Peter represents by his confession the type of person on which the true church will be built.

The first and second possibilities are often defended by pointing out that Peter’s name is _petros_ (small, loose rock) and the rock is _petra_ (bedrock). But this linguistic difference is not significant here and would be irrelevant if the conversation was originally in Aramaic. The second possibility is unlikely because Jesus describes Himself in this passage not as the foundation but as the builder of the church.

If it had not been for the abuse of this passage by the Roman Catholic Church, it is unlikely that any doubt would have arisen that the reference is to Peter. But the foundational rock is Peter as a representative apostle (v. 15 note), whose confession of Christ has been revealed to him by the Father. As Peter himself later declares (1 Pet. 2:4–8), all believers have become “living stones” by virtue of their association with Christ, with the apostles as the foundation because they receive and relay new covenant revelation (Eph. 2:20, 21; 3:5; Rev. 21:14). When Peter says that Jesus must not go to the cross, he is not called a foundation rock but a stumbling block (v. 23 and text note).

**church.** This term appears only twice in the Gospels (cf. 18:17) but often in the Epistles. In the Septuagint, it describes the “assembly” of Israel gathered in the Lord’s presence (Deut. 9:10; 10:4; 16:8; 18:16). Jesus implies His divine authority by promising to build “my church.”

**gates of hell.** In the OT and other literature, the “gates of Sheol” or the “gates of death” are equivalent to “death” (see, e.g., Ps. 107:18; Is. 38:10).

This metaphor specifies how the apostles are foundational to the church; they have been given binding and loosing powers, or “keys,” which lock and unlock doors. The apostles open the kingdom to those who share Peter’s confession and exclude those who will not receive their testimony to Christ (10:14, 15). The apostolic foundation of the church is laid in the written Word of God, the Scriptures, which are now the keys of Christ’s authority in the church (Eph. 2:20; 3:5) through the power of the Spirit (18:18). See theological note “Excommunication” on p. 1703.

See 8:4. In Jesus’ day, popular conceptions of the Messiah fail to acknowledge His suffering ministry, a concept that even Peter finds objectionable (16:21, 22) and all the disciples find distressing (17:23). To allow His disciples to proclaim His messiahship openly might instigate a political movement that will hamper His true redemptive mission (John 6:15).

This phrase marks a new phase of Jesus’ ministry (4:17 note). Matthew turns from Jesus’ public proclamation of the kingdom’s near approach to His careful instruction of the disciples that the kingdom must come through His death and resurrection, and the implications for His followers.

Simon is called “Peter” (rock) when he rightly confesses Jesus’ messiahship, but when he rejects Jesus’ forecast of His own suffering, Jesus labels Simon “Satan” (an opponent, but also mouthpiece of the Satan who earlier offered Jesus the world’s kingdoms without a cross; 4:8–10) and “hindrance” or “stumbling block” (text note)—a rock that could cause a fall and obstructs a path.

See note on 10:38. Here Jesus adds the command to deny oneself. The call to discipleship demands that one completely abandon the natural desire to seek comfort, fame, or power, and even the instinct to preserve one’s own life at all costs. The Messiah’s route of rejection and suffering blazes the trail for those who follow.

This statement is often interpreted as referring to the transfiguration (17:1, 2). Another possibility is the destruction of Jerusalem (10:23 note), but the context here is not focused on the judgment of Israel. The “coming” of the Son of Man more likely here relates to the entire process by which Jesus receives dominion, especially His resurrection, ascension, and sending of the Spirit at Pentecost. All these things happened during the lifetime of the disciples.

Such an exact time reference is rare in the Gospels; it seems to be included to show the connection between Peter’s confession at Caesarea Philippi and the transfiguration. Now that the disciples have begun to recognize who Jesus is, He moves toward the climactic events in Jerusalem. The transfiguration is part of Jesus’ preparation for that crisis.

Since the Law and the Prophets testify to Jesus, Moses the lawgiver, and Elijah, one of Israel’s greatest prophets, appear with Jesus. According to Luke 9:31, they discuss Jesus’ coming “departure” (Gk. _exodos_, referring to His death).

verse_quote: This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.
note:
The words from heaven, identical to those spoken by God the Father at Jesus’ baptism (3:17), interpret that radiance of Jesus’ face and clothing as a display of His divine glory as the unique and eternal Son (John 3:16).

**listen to him.** The word of God spoken through Moses and the prophets pointed to Jesus, and Moses predicted a prophet like himself, to whom Israel must listen (Deut. 18:15). Now the final word is spoken by and in the person of God’s Son (Heb. 1:1–4; John 1:1–18).
As in 16:20, Jesus’ true identity as divine Messiah is not to be divulged to those who seek only a political-military champion.

As Jesus taught in 11:14, John the Baptist was the fulfillment of Mal. 4:4–6, the prophecy cited by the scribes. Since both John the Baptist and the Son of Man did not fit common expectations, they were not recognized but rather rejected and ultimately killed.

The boy’s father uses a term (lit. “moon-struck”) that sums up a complex of symptoms without diagnosing whether the cause is physiological or spiritual. In this case, the boy’s uncontrollable bodily movements are attributable to a demon, which Jesus casts out (17:18).
Jesus, like Moses, comes down from the mount of glory to encounter unbelief (Ex. 32:15–21).

The disciples’ shortage of faith is not that they lack confidence or do not expect success—they are apparently surprised and distressed by their failure—but because their expectation is not properly grounded in dependence upon God. A tiny grain of true faith, rooted in submissiveness to God, is effective. Mark 9:29 makes this point even clearer by speaking of prayer as the key.

This statement is the second prediction of suffering and resurrection in Matthew (cf. 16:21–24). Jesus will undertake the suffering He describes as the servant of the Lord (Is. 53). Based on the disciples’ reaction, it appears that no one before Jesus ever identified the Messiah, the Son of Man, and the suffering servant of the OT as three titles of the one Redeemer King. The disciples are so distressed at the prospect of the Messiah’s suffering that they seem deaf to the promise of the resurrection. Even when it occurs, they do not initially believe it (28:17; Luke 24:8–11, 25, 37, 38)., 23

Again Jesus’ critics bring their complaint about Him to a disciple (cf. 9:10, 11). The passage is not about paying taxes to the civil authority (22:21) but about fulfilling a worship obligation to God. Jesus’ point is that the Christ and His disciples enjoy a relationship with God that frees them from the obligations imposed upon “others.” Yet Jesus, who has come not only to “fulfill all righteousness” (3:15) but also to fulfill the Law and the Prophets (5:17), complies with the law’s requirements in order to avoid giving offense. (The temple tax was prescribed in Ex. 30:13.) Paul advised (Rom. 14:13–21) and practiced (Acts 16:3; 21:26) similar continued observance of some ritual requirements of OT law to remove obstacles to his ministry among fellow Jews (1 Cor. 9:19–23).

This is the fourth of the five great teaching discourses in Matthew (Introduction: Characteristics and Themes; Literary Features). Jesus sets the tone for life in His church, where the smallest are honored and protected (18:1–9); sinners are treated as lost sheep to be found and as brothers to be reclaimed (18:10–20); and forgiveness flows freely and constantly to those who repent (18:21–35).
Jesus makes this comparison not because children are supposed to be innocent but because they depend upon others and humbly accept what they cannot provide for themselves.

Since Jesus’ followers must become “like children,” the “child” represents any disciple. Response to Jesus’ disciples is a response to Jesus Himself (see 25:31–46), and causing a disciple to sin is a grave offense, punishable by destruction far worse than physical death by drowning (v. 6; 10:28).
Universal human depravity will result in inevitable offenses, but individual responsibility (“woe to the one by whom the temptation comes”) is not diminished by the commonplace occurrence of sin.

Repeating His point from the Sermon on the Mount (5:29), Jesus insists that temptation to sin be resisted at all costs. Yet He has shown that the causes of sin are found not in the body’s members (hand, foot, eye) but in the hidden treasury of one’s heart (12:33–37; 15:17–20)., 9

Scripture teaches that angels guard and minister to God’s people (Ps. 91:11; Acts 12:15; Heb. 1:14) and that these spiritual beings may be assigned specific areas of responsibility (Dan. 12:1). God’s care of His people through angels should be an encouragement to Christians.

The concern for the one is not at the expense of the ninety-nine, but it indicates God’s commitment to each disciple and His special concern for one straying or in danger. God elects, seeks out, and preserves not only His church as a whole but also each individual within the church. For this reason, Jesus the Messiah associates with notorious “sinners” (Luke 15:1–7). His eagerness to seek the lost and His rejoicing when He finds the lost must be reflected in believers’ readiness to approach and correct a sinning brother in order to “gain” him (Matt. 18:15–17). God’s promise to intervene in person to retrieve His lost sheep (Ezek. 34:11–16) probably lies behind this parable (cf. John 10).

This three-stage procedure for dealing with a Christian in sin is at the heart of all church discipline. The goal is to bring about repentance while keeping general public awareness of the sin to a minimum. At no point is the matter to be broadcast to the world at large. See theological note “Excommunication” on previous page.

**you have gained your brother.** One’s motive and purpose in confronting a sinning believer must not be winning an argument, enforcing one’s rights, or venting a grievance, but restoring another member of God’s family, the church, to a reconciled relationship (cf. Gal. 6:1).

God’s law forbids convicting anyone on the testimony of a single witness (Deut. 17:6; 19:15), and the principle demanding multiple witnesses to substantiate evidence pervades Scripture (2 Cor. 13:1; 1 Tim. 5:19). Here, the witnesses’ first (and ideally only) role is to confirm the testimony of the offended brother in speaking to the offender, with a view toward his listening to the group and repenting, so that the dispute need not be brought to the church.

In the Gospels, Jesus uses the word “church” only here and in 16:18. As noted there, in the Septuagint the “assembly” of the people of God is called the _ekklēsia,_ or “church.” Jesus’ use of Deut. 19:15 in v. 16 implies that the church is equivalent to OT Israel.

**let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector.** Individuals who persist without repentance when the church itself confronts their obstinacy in sin are no longer to be regarded or treated as members of Christ’s church. Paul applies this discipline in 1 Cor. 5 and 1 Tim. 1:20.
See note on 16:19.

These verses should be taken in the larger context as still dealing with church discipline. Verse 19 is a further application of v. 18, and v. 20 states that Jesus is present among His people in a special way when the unity and purity of His family are at stake and when the church takes up the duty of discipline., 20

See 5:7 and 7:2. Those who know God’s mercy must operate on the principle of mercy. If they do not show mercy but insist on justice, they will not receive mercy, but justice. An unforgiving heart is an unforgiven heart and is subject to torment “until he should pay all” (v. 34; 6:12 note). A truly forgiving heart is one result of spiritual rebirth (John 3:3).

**18:21, 22 As many as seven times?** In view of the costly procedure that Jesus has laid out for our reclamation and recovery of brothers and sisters in sin, Peter wants to know the boundaries of his obligation to confront and forgive. Jesus’ “seventy times seven” vividly removes all limits to our obligation to forgive, setting a cap so high that score keeping is impossible. His parable then reveals the logic by which unimaginable divine forgiveness must evoke in its recipients an eager readiness to forgive the minor debts that we exact from one another., 22

A talent was the highest monetary unit of currency in first-century Judea, equivalent to six thousand denarii or drachmas (v. 28 note). Such a sum of money was practically uncountable, and a debt of this amount would not be repayable over many lifetimes. The debt of sin that all have incurred before God is utterly beyond our capacity to repay. The King’s cancellation of the debt is our only hope of escape.

The Roman denarius was a daily wage for workers (20:2) and was equivalent to the Gk. drachma (Acts 19:19). A hundred denarii, then, is not an insubstantial debt. Even so, the sum owed by the second servant to the first is nothing compared to the debt of the first servant to the king; it is less than one part in a hundred thousand.

The point of the parable is not that God’s forgiveness, once granted, will be revoked if a follower of Jesus refuses to forgive his brother or sister. Rather, refusal to forgive is symptomatic of a person who fails to grasp the impossible depth of his debt and the infinite magnitude of God’s mercy and therefore has no reason to presume that he has received God’s forgiveness in the first place.

The Pharisees’ question seems to reflect the opinion of Hillel, a rabbi who allowed divorce for the slightest reasons by interpreting “some indecency” in Deut. 24:1–4 very broadly. A rival teacher, Shammai, regarded only sexual unchastity as proper grounds. Jesus’ answer transcends this debate about the wording of Deuteronomy and returns to the order of creation by God (Gen. 2:24).

Hearing Jesus’ view of marriage, the Pharisees think they can set Him against Moses. But Jesus shows that Moses was not justifying divorce, much less “commanding” it, as the Pharisees claim. Rather, Moses’ regulation protected wives in the event of divorce. After a conditional statement (“if then”), Deut. 24:1–4 ends with the prohibition for a man to remarry a woman he had earlier divorced, treating her like property to be discarded and reacquired at will rather than as a person who is his partner by covenant. A hardness of heart with respect to marriage and divorce is specifically restrained by this case law., 8

The Gk. word for “sexual immorality” is broad, including a number of sexual sins besides adultery. In this clause (present also in 5:32 but omitted in Mark 10:11), Jesus recognizes that sexual infidelity strikes at the heart of the marital covenant between spouses and is therefore grounds for divorce. However, divorce is not mandatory, and reconciliation is desirable. See theological note “Divorce” on p. 1755.

verse_quote: it is better not to marry.
note: The disciples’ reaction seems both selfish and cynical. Jesus acknowledges that the lifelong commitment of marriage can only be fulfilled through God’s gifting and is not His calling to all. Some may be precluded from marriage by physical causes (eunuchs from birth or made so by men), but others pursue the single life by choice, for the sake of advancing God’s kingdom (cf. 1 Cor. 7:7–9).

The disciples view children as a distraction from the work of Jesus, but He welcomes them as subjects of the kingdom and blesses them. Since entrance into the kingdom is by God’s grace and not human achievement, dependent little ones have a special title to covenant blessing (18:1–9). Ironically, Jesus has called these very disciples “little children” to whom the Father reveals His secrets while hiding them from the wise (11:26, 27). See theological note “Infant Baptism” on p. 41.
This expression is equivalent to “enter the kingdom of God” (v. 24) and “be saved” (v. 25).

Jesus does not deny that He Himself is good (see Mark 10:17, 18; Luke 18:18, 19), nor that He can speak authoritatively about what is good. Rather, He challenges the superficial assumption behind the young man’s question—that he is quite capable of performing a good deed worthy of access into God’s kingdom. God’s law defines righteous behavior, so Jesus directs him first to a number of the Ten Commandments and the obligation to love one’s neighbor as oneself (Lev. 19:18; see Matt. 22:39).

Jesus’ instruction to the young man to sell all he has demonstrates that he is unwittingly in violation of the first commandment—“You shall have no other gods before me” (Ex. 20:3)—for he cannot bear to part with his wealth even for the sake of eternal life in the kingdom of God. What he lacks is the attitude that abandons everything (13:44, 45; 16:24–26) to receive God’s unearned grace (Phil. 3:7–9).

Wealth was considered evidence of God’s approval in Jesus’ day, and many Jews saw the rich as the likeliest candidates for the kingdom. Jesus turns this idea upside down, and the result is not lost on the disciples: “Who then can be saved?” (v. 25). Jesus responds that though the salvation of either rich or poor is humanly impossible, God can accomplish what human beings cannot. As Abraham, Sarah, and Mary discovered, nothing is too hard for the Lord (Gen. 8:14; Luke 1:37).
Governing, not sentencing to punishment.
The blessings of salvation far exceed anything that one must forsake to obtain them (1 Cor. 2:9).

Positions of honor or prestige in this life by no means assure heavenly approval; indeed, often the reverse is true. Jesus will soon show His competitive disciples that His own mission “not to be served, but to serve,” requires that in His kingdom leaders are those who serve as slaves (20:25–28). Similarly, as the following parable illustrates (20:1–16), the length of one’s earthly toil may not correspond to the amount of one’s heavenly reward, since the kingdom’s principle of recompense is not based on worldly concepts about rights but on divine mercy.

The repetition of the maxim of 19:30 in 20:16 (in inverted order) shows that Jesus is still addressing Peter’s expectation that the disciples’ sacrifice obligates God to repay them accordingly (19:27). This parable is a hard saying only for those who fail to recognize their absolute dependence on grace for any good thing from God’s hand. There is no room for a Christian to resent the good gifts God gives to another.

**20:1 vineyard.** Israel is symbolized as God’s vineyard in the OT (Ps. 80:8–13; Is. 3:14; 5:1–7) and in Jesus’ later parables (Matt. 21:28, 33). This symbolism and the apparent inequity of the workers’ compensation show that the story is not about workers’ rights in this world but about how mercy transcends mere justice in the kingdom of heaven.
A daily wage for farm workers, soldiers, and other hired laborers.
God’s law requires the prompt, daily compensation of day laborers (Lev. 19:13; Deut. 24:14, 15; cf. James 5:4).
See note on 19:30.

In this, Jesus’ third prediction of His passion and resurrection (16:21; 17:22, 23 notes), He adds the details that Jewish leaders will condemn Him to death and hand Him over to Gentiles, who will mock, flog, and then kill Him by crucifixion.

The request of the mother of James and John (see 4:21) on behalf of her sons is juxtaposed to Jesus’ announcement of His impending suffering to illustrate that His disciples have failed to understand the coming trauma despite His clear predictions (cf. Luke 18:34)., 21

In the OT, the “cup” normally signifies the outpouring of God’s wrath (Ps. 75:8; Is. 51:17, 22; Jer. 25:15, 16; see Rev. 16:19). That the disciples will drink this cup means they will experience suffering, but note that Jesus calls it “my cup.” Because Jesus drank the cup of God’s wrath, believers do not drink the wrath they deserve. In and through Christ’s suffering, they have already undergone judgment. They are now justified in Christ and heirs of His glory (Rom. 8:17). Yet their privilege is to be identified with Christ in His sufferings (Acts 9:4, 5; Col. 1:24; 1 Pet. 2:21).

**not mine to grant.** In the mystery of the Trinity, the Son is one with the Father in substance and equal to the Father in power and glory; yet He willingly submits to the Father’s will and defers to the Father’s authority as the incarnate, well-pleasing messianic Son, even in His exaltation (1 Cor. 15:28).

The indignation of the ten against James and John is another symptom of a competitive attitude and a preoccupation with personal rights and resistant to unmerited grace. In human social hierarchies, rulers’ whims are fulfilled by those they lead; but in Jesus’ kingdom, leaders serve as slaves because the King Himself, the Son of Man who now has universal authority (Dan. 7:13, 14), came to serve, even to the point of death (see Phil. 2:5–11).

This term refers to the price paid to deliver someone from slavery or imprisonment. The price of freedom from sin and condemnation is Jesus’ life, given for us (1 Pet. 1:18, 19). Since the elect are ransomed from the wrath of God, the ransom was offered to God Himself. Jesus drinks the cup of God’s wrath (v. 23) not for His own sins but as the means of ransoming many.

**for many.** The Gk. preposition translated “for” can also be translated “in the place of.” It expresses the substitutionary nature of Jesus’ suffering. That Jesus says “many” here, alluding to Is. 53:11, 12, implies a definite, personal focus to His redemptive mission, and an atonement that is made for a specific people (cf. Matt. 26:28). Nevertheless, He dies for “many” and not “a few.” See notes on John 17:9; 1 Tim. 2:6.

Luke says they were entering Jericho rather than leaving. One possibility is that Matthew and Mark refer to the ruins of OT Jericho, about a mile (1.6 km) away from the newer town of Jericho built by Herod (Luke 18:35 note).

Once again Matthew mentions two men, where Mark and Luke mention only the (perhaps more vocal and insistent) son of Timaeus (8:28 note). The healing of the blind—a miracle unprecedented in the OT (John 9:32)—will be attested by two witnesses.

verse_quote: What do you want me to do for you?
note: Although Zebedee’s two sons would not receive their request for positions of honor, the Son of Man, who came to serve, grants the request of two helpless, nameless blind men who plead for His mercy.

Of the Synoptic Gospels, only Matthew mentions the colt’s mother, probably to emphasize that it was a young colt, not yet weaned and therefore not yet ridden (cf. Mark 11:2), and because the quotation from Zech. 9:9 prophesies that the coming king would ride on “a colt, the foal of a donkey.” Jesus chooses to make the fulfillment of prophecy unmistakable.

The triumphal entry is a symbolic act. Zech. 9:9 was recognized as messianic by Jews, and the shout “Hosanna to the Son of David!” (v. 9) as well as the spreading of cloaks on the ground (cf. 2 Kin. 9:13) indicates that the crowd recognizes Jesus’ claim to be the Messiah. Note David’s proclamation of Solomon as his designated heir by having him ride into the city on a donkey (1 Kin. 1:33, 38, 44).
Jesus rode the colt (Mark 11:2). “Them” probably refers to the garments, the closest antecedent in the sentence.

A Hb. expression meaning, “Save!” drawn by the crowds from Ps. 118:25, which speaks of the Messiah’s entering the gates of righteousness (vv. 19, 20) to the acclamation of his subjects, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” (v. 26).

Although His authoritative teaching and miracles showed that Jesus was “a prophet mighty in deed and word” (Luke 24:19; Matt. 14:5; 21:26; cf. Deut. 18:15), the crowds’ reception of Him as the long-awaited Son of David had unmistakable royal overtones.

John 2:13–22 recounts a cleansing of the temple early in Jesus’ ministry rather than during the final week. Many scholars, both liberal and conservative, propose that either John or the Synoptic Gospels modified the order or chronology of this event for theological reasons. Others believe that Jesus purged the temple of commercialism early in His public ministry and found it necessary to drive out money-changers again in the week that ended in His death (Mark 11:15 note).

**21:13 a house of prayer.** Money-changers who exchanged Roman coins, bearing the emperor’s image (22:20, 21), for the temple shekel in which God’s tithe could be paid, as well as those who sold pigeons certified as “clean” for the purposes of sacrifice, provided convenient services to Jewish worshipers. But the location of their commerce, in the court of the Gentiles, contradicted God’s purpose for the temple: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples” (Is. 56:7).

**den of robbers.** The phrase is from Jer. 7:11, where the Lord denounced the idea prevalent in ancient Judah that the physical temple guaranteed His blessing in spite of Judah’s wickedness.

Jesus’ quotation of Ps. 8:2 to justify the children’s praises is astounding, for Ps. 8 says that God has ordained worship for Himself from the lips of children. Thus Jesus claims the prerogative of deity.

Matthew condenses an incident that actually takes place on two separate days (cf. Mark 11:12–14, 20–26). The linking of the symbolic miracle of judgment with the cleansing of the temple implies God’s imminent punishment of Israel by the destruction of the city and the temple. Speaking through the prophet Jeremiah many centuries before this event, God compared Israel’s unfaithfulness to a fig tree that bears no figs (Jer. 8:13) and to inedible figs that will be thrown away as garbage (24:1–10).

This statement is similar to 17:20, but here the emphasis is on not doubting. Freedom from doubt arises from confidence in God’s boundless power and an awareness that one’s request aligns with God’s will. Such faith receives what it asks for; trust in God is not presumptive arrogance but submission to His will., 22

When the chief priest and elders questioned Jesus’ authority to cleanse the temple of commercial enterprises that interfere with worship, He challenges them to identify whether John the Baptist was a true prophet whose authority was from heaven (God) or a false prophet who spoke presumptuously (cf. Deut. 18:20–22). They cannot publicly grant John’s prophetic authority, which the crowd recognizes, without answering their own question about the authority of Jesus, to whom John testified (3:11–17). Although Jesus refuses to answer their question directly, the following parable of the tenants implies His answer.

Though simpler than the well-known parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:11–32), this parable makes a similar point: tax collectors and prostitutes, whose lifestyles defied God’s law, repented of their sin and returned to the Lord in response to John the Baptist’s preaching, whereas Judaism’s leaders, who professed devotion to God’s revealed will, refused to heed John’s testimony to the Messiah and consequently stayed outside God’s kingdom and its joys.

This parable is based on Is. 5:1–7 and possibly also Is. 3:13–15 and Ps. 80:8–18. The meaning is clear: the landowner is God; the vineyard is the kingdom of God (v. 43); the servants are the prophets; the son is Jesus; the tenants are the Jewish leaders who oppose Jesus; the killing of the son is the crucifixion; and the removal of the tenants is the transferal of the kingdom to a new people of God that includes Gentiles, a people led by the apostles who are “tenants who will give him the fruits in their seasons” (Matt. 21:41; 1 Cor. 3:5–9). 2 Chr. 36:15, 16 cites Judah’s mocking rejection of the many messengers (prophets) whom God sent as the final reason for the exile.

In response to the challenge to His authority (v. 23), Jesus quotes Ps. 118:22, 23 as evidence that His authority, like John’s, is given by God rather than derived from human institutions. At His triumphal entry the crowds quoted vv. 25, 26 of this psalm.

This saying combines the prophecies of Is. 8:14 and Dan. 2:34, 44. Jesus claims to be the destroyer of earthly kingdoms, the founder of God’s kingdom on earth. The Jewish leaders are, as prophesied, opposed to this kingdom. Jesus’ quotation of Ps. 118 in v. 42 and the allusion to Is. 8:14 and Dan. 2 provide the ground for the “stone” as a reference to Christ that appears frequently in the NT (Acts 4:11; Rom. 9:33; 1 Pet. 2:6–8). The reference to Ps. 118 (“the cornerstone”) and Is. 8:14 (“stone”) are OT contextual references to God’s being a temple of blessing for some but a judgment to others. Likewise, the “stone” of Dan. 2 symbolizes a judgment for evil kingdoms but grew to “fill the whole earth” as God’s universal temple (cf. Is. 2:2), which was an implied blessing (cf. allusion to Gen. 1:28) for the members of the kingdom. Jesus applies all these temple references to Himself, so that He is the fulfillment of everything toward which the OT temples pointed, either for blessing or judgment.

Although there are similarities between this parable and Luke 14:16–24, there are few verbal parallels and significant differences. As a skilled teacher, Jesus adapts a common plot line to different occasions.

**22:1–10** The first part of the parable continues the theme that the heirs of the kingdom have rejected it and the kingdom is being offered to others. God’s servants now offer the gospel not only to Israel but to all sorts of people (v. 9).

An advance invitation notifying the guests of the date of a formal banquet such as a wedding feast is followed on the day itself with notification that the dinner was ready to be served, so invitees should come immediately. Having foretold the coming of His kingdom in OT prophecy, God is now inviting Israel to celebrate its arrival in the person of His Son.

The second part of the parable, not found in Luke 14, affirms that receiving an invitation to God’s kingdom does not guarantee inclusion. Although everyone who hears the gospel has been invited, and although many may claim to be in the kingdom, only those clothed appropriately will enjoy the king’s hospitality. The wedding garment may symbolize the gift of Christ’s righteousness (Rev. 3:18; 6:11; 7:13, 14; 19:8; cf. Zech. 3:3–5) or the truth that genuine faith, in contrast to its counterfeit, will bear fruit in obedient living (Matt. 7:21–23).
A description of eternal punishment. There will be no middle ground between heaven and hell.

Only those who are chosen will be seated at the marriage supper of the Lamb, and this election does not depend on any previous ethnic or moral status (8:11, 12). See theological note “Effectual Calling” on p. 2146.

verse_quote: plotted how to entangle him in his words.
note: In a series of exchanges, various religious and political parties in first-century Judaism pose questions to Jesus that they believe will confront Him with unanswerable dilemmas and discredit His authority as a teacher. The Pharisees with the Herodians ask His view on paying the Roman poll tax (22:15–22); the Sadducees offer a test case that tries to show the absurdity of bodily resurrection (22:23–33); and the Pharisees ask Jesus to elevate one of God’s commands above the others (22:34–40). Then Jesus turns the tables and challenges them to admit that Ps. 110 promises that the Messiah, though David’s descendant, is also David’s superior (22:41–46).

The hated poll tax symbolized submission to Rome. If Jesus simply advocates payment of the tax, He will alienate the people; if He encourages nonpayment, the Herodians will accuse Him of treason against the empire.

The Roman denarius bears an image of the reigning Caesar and declares him to be a son of the gods, violating the first and second commandments. Jesus’ answer turns the question to a deeper issue than one’s relationship to political institutions, pagan or otherwise. Jesus calls for ultimate allegiance to God. The coin bearing the image of Caesar belongs to him; human beings made in the image of God belong to God.

**22:21 to Caesar.** See theological note “Civil Government” on p. 2004.

The Sadducees, who controlled administration of the temple, accepted only the five books of Moses as fully authoritative. Because they did not find explicit mention of a future bodily resurrection in Moses, they rejected this doctrine (Acts 4:2; 23:6–8), which was taught overtly in later OT books (Dan. 12:2) and held by the Pharisees.

Jesus quotes from the Pentateuch (Ex. 3:6), a portion of Scripture particularly valued by the Sadducees. That God “is” (not “was”) the God of the patriarchs proclaims the resurrection, for “He is not God of the dead, but of the living.” The eternal God calls His saints to an eternal relationship with Himself. All this implies that the patriarchs continue to live in the presence of God and will be resurrected in the future. Death cannot have the last word over those who are in a saving relationship to God by His grace., 32

Jesus quotes the command to love God with all one’s being, which flows from the _Shema_, Israel’s ancient confession that her God is one (Deut. 6:4, 5). Rabbinic scholars in the first century recognized the supremacy and centrality of the obligation to love God unreservedly and preeminently (Luke 10:25–28). See theological note “Love” on p. 2036.

verse_quote: all the Law and the Prophets.
note: A way of referring to the entire OT. Love fulfills the law because it sums up God’s commandments and motivates obedience to them (Rom. 13:8–10; 1 Cor. 13). It does not dissolve God’s norms for conduct but illumines them and displays their depths (5:17; Rom. 8:4). See theological note “The Law of God” on p. 124.

The Pharisees had tested Jesus; now Jesus tests them. He focuses on the crucial issue—the identity of the Messiah (Christ)—and His quotation from Ps. 110 shows that the common view of the Messiah as merely a human descendant of David is insufficient. Sons are subordinate to their fathers, yet David “in the Spirit” (by divine inspiration) referred to the ultimate king, who would be his “son” (2 Sam. 7:12, 13), as “my Lord.”

**Christ.** See note on 1:1.

Having silenced His opponents who controlled Judaism’s religious establishment, Jesus brings Israel’s prophetic tradition to a climax (cf. 21:33–46) by delivering oracles of woe to the nation’s unfaithful leaders (vv. 13–36 note). Their disregard for God’s righteousness, thinly disguised by hypocrisy, is the reason for the impending doom of Jerusalem, announced in the language of OT prophecy (23:37, 38).

Though Jesus elsewhere condemns the scribes and Pharisees for adding human tradition to the law and for evading the spirit of the law (vv. 13–32; 15:1–9; cf. 5:20–48), here He recognizes the legitimate teaching office that they occupy in His context (Deut. 17:8–13).
See theological note “Legalism.”
See note on Ex. 13:9.

In forbidding the use of the titles “rabbi,” “teacher” (v. 8), “father” (v. 9), and “instructors” (lit. “leaders,” v. 10), Jesus does not prohibit organization or the use of all titles in the church (cf. Acts 20:17; 1 Cor. 9:1; 1 Tim. 3:1, 2, 8, 12; Titus 1:5–7). His warning is against the temptation to claim for oneself authority and honor that belong uniquely to God and His Christ.

Luke 11:37–54 records an earlier proclamation of six woes. This series of seven woes is a prophetic pronouncement, for it brings God’s lawsuit against His people and announces the imminent realization of the covenant curses (cf. Is. 5:8–23; Hab. 2:6–20), especially against Israel’s unfaithful shepherds (Jer. 23:1–6; Ezek. 34). Leaders of the covenant community are judged more strictly because their words and example influence so many others, for good or ill (James 3:1).

**23:13 hypocrites.** See note on 6:2.

**shut the kingdom.** The teachers of the law and Pharisees do this by turning people away from Christ and His righteousness. The disciples are to do the opposite, freely proclaiming the gospel.

See note on 5:22. Scribes intent on establishing their own righteousness through their keeping the law produce converts who are equally resistant to God’s gift of righteousness by faith alone (Rom. 10:3, 4).
See 5:33–37. This way of taking oaths signals that one has no intention of keeping them. God desires truth in all our words (5:37).

Drawing distinctions between physical elements (the temple or its gold, the altar or its sacrifice) when making an oath obscures the reality that God Himself is invoked as witness to the oath. He who indwells the earthly temple and always occupies His heavenly throne will impose sanctions on those who evade the solemn commitments that they have uttered in His hearing.

Tithing should be an expression of compassion for those dependent on others: Levites, orphans, widows, and sojourners (Num. 14:28, 29; 26:12–15); but the Pharisees’ scrupulous tithing of spices to the neglect of the weightier matters of the law ignores the rationale behind the commandment: justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
The gnat is the smallest unclean animal, and the camel is the largest. In Aramaic, the two words sound similar.

Abel was the first person to be killed for righteousness’s sake (Gen. 4:8). The identity of Zechariah is uncertain. Zechariah the prophet was the “son of Barachiah,” but there is no evidence that he was martyred. Josephus mentions a Zechariah, son of Baruch, who was killed by Zealots in the temple area. Zechariah, son of Jehoiada, is the last martyr mentioned in the OT in the Hb. canonical order (2 Chr. 24:20–22). He was killed in the temple courtyard by command of Joash. If not for the words “son of Barachiah,” the Zechariah of 2 Chr. 24 would be most likely, since Abel and Zechariah are the first and last martyrs in the Hb. canon. It is possible that “son of Barachiah” was an insertion by an early copyist (Luke 11:51 does not have it).

**whom you murdered.** By persecuting Christ, the Pharisees become identified with their murderous ancestors, as He had charged in the parable of the tenants (21:33–46). Stephen will later make the same connection (Acts 7:51–53).
The punishment that “this generation” experiences is the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple in A.D. 70. See note on 24:34.

verse_quote: How often would I have gathered your children.
note: Jesus again claims implicitly to be God Himself by alluding to Scripture’s comparison of the Lord’s protection of His people to that of a mother bird sheltering chicks under her wings (Deut. 32:11; Pss. 17:8; 36:7; 91:4). His lament over unbelieving Israel is genuine, for God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezek. 18:23; 33:11), even though their sin is ordained in His sovereign plan (Matt. 26:24; Luke 22:22). In particular, in vv. 37, 38 Jesus is addressing Jerusalem’s leaders who have not cared for her children in the way they should. Indeed, their ungodly influence has resulted in Jerusalem’s children not wanting to be “gathered in” by Jesus. Jesus wants to “gather in” the children of Jerusalem, but the leaders are “unwilling” to let Him do that.

verse_quote: you will not see me again, until.
note: Some interpret this verse as a promise of an end-time conversion of the Jews (Rom. 11:25–32 and note), though the context seems to point more to the judgment of national Israel and the extension of the promises to spiritual Israel, made up of Gentiles as well as Jews (v. 38; cf. 21:43). Even if this latter interpretation of this verse is correct, it does not preclude the conversion of a substantial number of Jews to Christ prior to His return, as other NT passages seem to indicate as much (Rom. 11:25–32 note).

These two chapters are the last of Jesus’ five great discourses in Matthew. Sometimes called the Olivet Discourse because of its setting, most of the discourse is also recorded in Mark 13. The language is symbolic, and it deals with a number of events, not just a single incident.

There are three basic interpretive approaches to this discourse. (1) All or most of ch. 24 (at least through v. 35) is concerned exclusively with the destruction of Jerusalem, and the coming of the Son of Man (24:30) is the ascension and coronation of Jesus in heaven. (2) All of the sermon is about the second coming of Christ in judgment. (3) The sermon combines the destruction of Jerusalem announced by Jesus (24:1, 2) and the “close of the age,” with which His disciples associate that traumatic judgment (24:3). Although it is sometimes difficult to separate the references to the events surrounding the fall of Jerusalem and the second coming, Jesus Himself distinguishes and separates them by giving signs to prepare His followers for Jerusalem’s destruction within “this generation” (24:15–28, 32–35), while stressing that the arrival of “that day and hour” (of His glorious bodily return) will not be predictable even by His disciples, so they must be prepared for His arrival at any time (24:36–50).
This was fulfilled during the Roman conquest of Jerusalem in A.D. 70 (Mark 13:2 note).

Wars, earthquakes, persecutions, and false prophets are all signs of Jesus’ coming, but they indicate only the certainty of judgment, not its timing (vv. 6, 8). Such signs characterize the entire period between His resurrection and His coming in judgment. Knowing when Jesus will return might lead His disciples to laziness and laxity in their watchfulness. The “when” (v. 3) that Jesus gives is task-oriented: it is after the gospel has been preached to the nations by His disciples (v. 14).
The Great Commission that the risen Christ will give His church will be fulfilled (Matt. 28:18–20).

Although some interpreters take this passage to refer exclusively to the second coming, there are unmistakable references to the destruction of Jerusalem in A.D. 70, as is clear from the parallel account in Luke 21:20–24. The destruction of Jerusalem—its “house ...left desolate,” which Jesus has just lamented (Matt. 23:38)—is a foretaste of the last judgment and so is a sign of the coming wrath. It stands as a unique declaration of the end of the old age, and so is a specific and uniquely important sign.

**24:15 abomination of desolation.** In Dan. 9:27; 11:31 the phrase refers to the desecration of the temple by the Syrian ruler Antiochus IV Epiphanes. In 168 B.C., Antiochus erected a pagan altar in the temple. According to Josephus, he also sacrificed swine there. Shortly before A.D. 70, the Zealots entered the temple precincts during the war with Rome, and their presence could have been considered a desecration. In A.D. 70, the Romans entered the temple with military standards, ceremonial insignia that were elements of their religion. Reliefs on the Arch of Titus in Rome show Roman troops removing the temple’s sacred vessels, including the lampstand, after which they burned the temple.

**let the reader understand.** The sense is not “whoever reads this gospel,” but “whoever reads Daniel.” Antiochus’s blasphemous assault on God’s temple, prophesied in Daniel, foreshadowed the temple’s utter destruction by Rome only a few decades after Jesus spoke these words.
According to the early church historian Eusebius, the Christians did flee Jerusalem during the Jewish War in obedience to a prophecy.
Although this verse is usually taken with vv. 15–21, it is also possible to understand it as reverting to the general “beginning of the birth pains” of vv. 4–14.

Although the false prophets will try to deceive the elect, there is no real possibility that they will succeed. God will keep the elect secure in His love (Rom. 8:31–39; cf. John 10:28, 29). See theological note “Perseverance of the Saints” on p. 1994.

As traumatic as the sufferings of A.D. 70 will be, the disciples should not be alarmed by reports that their Lord has returned in some secret way or in some secret place. The coming of Christ will be unambiguous and evident to all.

This proverb may reinforce the announcement that Jesus’ second coming will be public and unmistakable; or, since the word “vultures” can also refer to eagles (which also eat carrion), an emblem of the Roman Empire, it may mean that the convergence of Roman troops on Jerusalem and its temple will signal the death of a covenant people who have refused their Messiah and the transfer of God’s kingdom to a new, international “Israel” that fulfills all that the old covenant people were supposed to be (21:43).

Some have understood these verses to represent the defeat of Satan’s forces, the Son of Man’s vindication, and the spread of the gospel to all the world as having occurred symbolically at the destruction of Jerusalem. But the language of v. 31 is parallel to passages such as 13:41; 16:27; 25:31, 1 Cor. 15:52; and 1 Thess. 4:14–17. The passage most naturally refers to the second coming. On this reading, “immediately” is not intended to set a date for the coming of the Son of Man (which would contradict 24:36), but to indicate that Jerusalem’s destruction is closely linked to the second coming in God’s purposes, although the temporal distance between them cannot be discerned by human beings.

Christ Himself, or the first moments of His appearing.

**mourn.** The mourning of the nations is an allusion to Zech. 12:10–12, and the coming on the clouds refers to Christ’s assumption of dominion prophesied in Dan. 7:13, 14.

The phrase naturally means the people living as Jesus spoke. Some, however, suggest that it means “this race,” or “this sort of people,” that is, evil and adulterous people (cf. 12:39).

**all these things.** That is, “all these things” referred to in v. 33 (and vv. 2, 3), which are distinguished from the consummation itself. They are the “beginning of the birth pains” (v. 8) and signs that foreshadow the final coming of Christ, including the siege and fall of Jerusalem. All of the elements of this prophecy, except for the second coming itself, occurred in some form before every member of the Twelve died (Luke 21:32 note).

This remains true, and after His resurrection, Jesus reaffirms the truth that it is not given to humans to know “times or seasons” that have been fixed by the Father (Acts 1:7). Although this discourse gives disciples signs by which they could anticipate Jerusalem’s fall, “that day and hour” (of His second coming) cannot be predicted by humans. He will come like a thief “at an hour you do not expect” (vv. 43, 44, 50; 1 Thess. 5:1–3; Rev. 3:3). Throughout the NT, our Lord and His apostles consistently rebuke attempts to predict the time of His second or final coming.

**nor the Son.** Although omniscient with respect to His deity, with respect to His humanity Jesus’ knowledge is both finite and changeable (Luke 2:52). Mysteriously, His two natures are united in one person, yet their distinctive attributes are not mixed or confused. See theological note “The Humanity of Christ” on p. 2279.

An active state, not passive waiting, according to vv. 45–51.

**is coming.** See theological note “The Return of Christ” on p. 2137.

Members of the church, especially leaders “set over his household,” exhibit genuine faith when they remain faithful to their tasks despite the delay of Christ’s return. Those who abuse their authority in the master’s absence, revealing their unbelief in His promise, will be caught unaware by His coming and condemned to His severest condemnation and punishment.
The delay of Christ’s return distinguishes the wise from the foolish. Being ready means being prepared for a long delay; short-lived zeal is inadequate.

verse_quote: all became drowsy and slept ... some of your oil.
note: These details belong to the parable’s social setting and narrative movement. They should not be allegorized (even wise virgins sleep, and even the foolish find oil to buy). Instead, the story makes a single point: when the bridegroom arrives, it will be too late to prepare to welcome him.
The highest unit of currency known to Jesus’ hearers. See notes on 18:24, 28. The English word _talent_, meaning a natural endowment or special ability, is derived from this parable.
In the ancient world, burying money or valuables was considered a responsible way to keep it safe.

verse_quote: I knew you to be a hard man.
note: The third servant tries to excuse his excessive caution by alleging his master’s demanding character and claiming that he was afraid to risk the loss of the talent entrusted to him. In fact, his inaction stems from sloth and indifference to his master’s interests, so he deserves expulsion from the master’s employment and protection “into the outer darkness” (v. 30).

Jesus’ announcement of His coming in glory to judge all the nations, like a shepherd dividing sheep from goats, resumes the theme of the parable of the weeds sown among wheat (13:24–30, 36–43) and the parable of the net (13:47–50). It also repeats the idea that He counts treatment meted out to His “little ones” (His disciples) as treatment of Himself (10:40–42).

**Son of Man.** On this title, see note on 8:20. The influence of Daniel’s vision of “one like a son of man” who approaches the Ancient of Days in clouds of glory to receive end-time dominion (Dan. 7:13, 14) appears throughout this final discourse of Jesus (24:30, 31, 36, 37).
The image of God’s people as sheep is found in Ezek. 34 and is integral to Jesus’ teaching about His strong care for His followers (10:16; 18:12; see 9:36; John 10).

God’s kingdom is bestowed by grace on the poor in spirit (5:3; 18:3, 4). The kindness that the sheep show to Jesus’ needy brothers (v. 40 note) does not merit this reward but reveals that their hearts have been transformed by His mercy.

verse_quote: the least of these my brothers.
note: Jesus cared for the needy in general (4:24) and calls His disciples to do the same (10:8; 19:21). However, in this scene of the last judgment, Jesus’ “brothers” are His disciples (10:42; 12:48, 49), to whom He has revealed the Father (11:25–27) and whom He has taught to pray to God as Father (6:6–15). The judgment of the nations will depend on how they have responded to Christians who bear the gospel (10:40–42). Christ identifies with His people. Their suffering is His suffering (Acts 9:4 note), and compassion shown to them is compassion shown to Him.
See theological note “Hell” on p. 1753.
This formula concludes each of the five main discourses in Matthew (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1). See Introduction: Literary Features.

Although the officials expect to postpone the murder of Jesus until after Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread (Mark 14:1 note), God’s purpose (v. 2) is for it to coincide with the feast (v. 17 note). Jesus will die as the fulfillment of the Passover lamb, whose blood protects God’s people from death (1 Cor. 5:7, 8; Rev. 5:6–10).

Many parallels with Mark 14:3–9 and John 12:1–8 (Bethany, costly perfume, criticism of the woman for waste, Jesus’ defense of her and assurance that her act will be remembered) show that the three passages recount the same incident. Mark agrees with Matthew’s account regarding the time (two days before Passover; cf. Mark 14:1) and the method of anointing (on Jesus’ head). John differs chronologically (six days before Passover) and records that Mary anointed His feet. Although certain details differ, none necessarily conflict (John 12:3 note). Luke 7:36–38, however, records a different incident earlier in Jesus’ ministry in which His host is a Pharisee, not a leper, and the objection concerns the sinfulness of the woman rather than the cost of the ointment.
John reports the hypocritical objection of Judas (John 12:4–6) and Matthew indicates that the others agree with John’s assessment.

Care for the poor, who are always “with you,” is commanded by God (Deut. 15:11). But the commandment cannot have a higher priority than Jesus, the One sent by the author of the commandment. Similarly, God commands honor of father and mother but not above honor to Jesus (10:37; 15:4–6; 19:29).

verse_quote: the first day of Unleavened Bread.
note:
The day of preparation for Passover, presumably 14 Nisan (the first month of the Jewish calendar). Jesus celebrated Passover that evening, 15 Nisan, and was crucified the next afternoon—the same day, since days start at sundown in Jewish reckoning. The gospel of John seems to present Jesus as crucified on the day before the temple leadership and the populace of Jerusalem observed the Passover (John 18:28; 19:14, 31).

Calvin understood preparation day to be the day before Passover and argued that the Jews, according to some traditions, combined the Passover with the weekly Sabbath (John 19:14 note). In that case, Matt. 27:62 would refer to the preparation day observed by the Jewish leadership. There is some difficulty, however, in seeing how Jesus’ disciples could have had their lamb slaughtered in advance of the official schedule, and Mark 14:12 states that Jesus arranged to observe the Passover on the evening of the day when the lambs were customarily slaughtered. Alternatively, some have suggested that because of the number of pilgrims in Jerusalem at the Passover, some Jews sacrificed the lamb they ate for the Passover meal a day before the official day of slaughter. Whatever the solution, Matthew and Mark clearly identify the meal that Jesus ate with His disciples on the eve of His crucifixion as the Passover meal (John 19:14 note).

Again Jesus emphasizes that all the terrible events soon to take place are totally under God’s control. The gospel of John makes the same point by speaking repeatedly of Jesus’ death as His “hour” (John 2:4; 7:30; 8:20; 12:23, 27; 13:1; 17:1).

See note on 8:20.

**as it is written of him.** Jesus’ atoning death was not merely the tragic result of an evil human conspiracy. The event and its circumstances, including betrayal by His friend (Pss. 41:9; 55:12–14), were planned by God since before the world was formed and were revealed in the OT Scriptures. Nevertheless, those who brought about Jesus’ death remain responsible for their actions (“woe to that man”; cf. Acts 2:23).

In the old covenant, the Passover meal commemorated Israel’s deliverance from Egypt. By transforming His last Passover meal to institute the Lord’s Supper, Jesus shows the consistent focus on redemption throughout God’s revelation. The Lord’s Supper demonstrates the essential continuity between the old and the new covenants by revealing that the true meaning of the Passover lies in the deliverance effected by Jesus’ death (1 Cor. 5:7, 8).

**26:26 this is my body.** In Roman Catholicism, these words are quoted in support of the doctrine of transubstantiation, which teaches that though the outward, physical attributes of the bread and wine remain unchanged, the invisible essence is transformed into the body and blood of Christ. Calvin and the other Reformers recognized that the elements _represent_ Christ’s body and blood, while they found it difficult to come to agreement on what exactly this representation means. Jesus utters these words while physically present with His disciples, so the bread and cup that He holds are obviously distinct from, not identical to, the body in which He will soon suffer on the cross. The bread and wine are more than symbols, however, for through the Holy Spirit Jesus will come to His church to communicate _tangibly_ the saving benefits of His grace, which are _heard_ in the gospel (1 Cor. 10:16). See theological note “The Lord’s Supper” on p. 2032.

The Mosaic covenant was inaugurated with sacrificial blood that symbolized the deadly curse that would ensue if Israel were to violate its commitment to the Lord (Ex. 24:8). The new covenant prophesied by Jeremiah (Jer. 31:31–34; cf. Luke 22:17–20; 1 Cor. 11:23–25) is inaugurated by the sacrifice of Christ, who endured the curse on behalf of His unfaithful people, thereby guaranteeing their inheritance of the blessings of the covenant (Heb. 7:22; 9:15, 16; 12:24; 13:20, 21). The Lord’s Supper symbolizes and seals to believers Christ’s covenant inauguration and fulfillment in their behalf. See theological note “The Sacraments” on p. 1726.

verse_quote: new with you in my Father’s kingdom.
note: Jesus’ temporary abstinence entails the promise that His death will not be the end of His communion with His disciples, reaffirming His predictions that He will rise from the dead and return to restore their joy (16:21; 17:23; 20:19; John 14:18; 16:16–22).

In the context of Zech. 13:7, the Lord strikes the shepherd, the “man who stands next to me,” and God’s “little ones” are scattered. Subsequently they are renewed and truly become God’s people. The disciples’ desertion of Jesus represents Israel’s apostasy**.**

See note on 20:23. Jesus is horrified at the prospect of enduring His Father’s wrath. Jesus has to face death knowing that His Father will not be with Him but against Him in the wrath of judgment.

**not as I will, but as you will.** In His utter innocence, Jesus is appropriately repulsed not just by the agonizing death that awaits Him but by the prospect of being identified with human sin and guilt; yet His resolve to obey the Father by completing His costly redemptive mission does not falter even at this point of utmost testing (Heb. 5:7–10; 10:5–10).

Jesus had taught His disciples to pray, “Lead us not into temptation” (6:13), but at the crucial moment, they failed to ask God for the strength to stand against Satan’s power, which was superior to theirs but not to God’s (1 Cor. 10:13; Eph. 6:10–12, 18–20).
David’s lament, that a close friend with whom he had shared bread had betrayed him, is thus fulfilled (Ps. 41:9; John 13:18).

verse_quote: Put your sword back into its place.
note: Jesus does not bring His kingdom with force, as earthly kings do (John 18:36). Compare David’s rebuke to a loyal defender, Abishai (2 Sam. 16:9–12).

Since God had protected Israel (Ex. 14:19, 20; Ps. 34:7) and ancient prophets such as Elisha (2 Kin. 6:17) with His angels, surely the beloved Son could request such defenders from His Father if it had been consistent with His fulfillment of God’s plan revealed in “the Scriptures.”

**26:54, 56 be fulfilled.** Jesus knows that the Scriptures prophesying salvation through His death must be fulfilled (Luke 22:37). Some commentators suggest that Zech. 13:7 is still in view (v. 31), since at this point “the disciples left him and fled,” scattered like sheep. Jesus is probably referring broadly to His death and resurrection (see Luke 24:44–46)., 56

The Sanhedrin had difficulty finding false witnesses whose testimonies coincided with and supported a verdict that would justify execution. Finally they used a charge based on a distortion of something Jesus had said (John 2:19), which they construed as a prophecy of the destruction of the temple complex on Mount Zion (see Matt. 24:1, 2, 15) and blasphemy against God Himself (see Acts 6:11–14). The numerous irregularities in this trial are not evidence of historical unreliability but of the extreme and desperate actions that the Jewish leaders took to rid themselves of Jesus. The testimony of the “witnesses” about Jesus’ statement is false for at least two reasons: (1) Their statement obviously intends that Jesus was speaking about the literal architectural temple of Israel that He would purportedly destroy and rebuild. But in the true testimony in John 2:19–22, Jesus affirms that His body is the temple that will be destroyed and which He Himself will raise up. (2) Also, according to John 2:19–22, Jesus did not say that He would destroy the temple but that the Jews would destroy the temple, which is His own person.

The suffering servant was silent like a lamb led to slaughter (Is. 53:7). His calm refusal to defend Himself against false accusations will later astonish the Roman governor (Matt. 27:14).

**I adjure you.** Jesus does not answer, and Caiaphas invokes the presence of God to force Him to respond: Does Jesus claim to be the Messiah sent from God?

Jesus’ answer is affirmative though indirect, probably because the high priest’s understanding of the Messiah’s role is so different from the role Jesus actually fulfills. Jesus responds in the same way to a similar question from Pilate in 27:11.

**from now on you will see.** Jesus probably speaks of the process of exaltation to the right hand of the Father that begins with His humiliation and death. The Jewish leaders will soon “see” in the resurrection reports of the soldiers (28:11–15) and Stephen’s eyewitness testimony of the majesty of the exalted Christ (Acts 7:56) that the one whom they had killed is the Messiah He claimed to be. At Pentecost some fifty days later, the descent of the Spirit, which enables believers to proclaim God’s mighty works in the tongues of the nations, will give evidence of Jesus’ heavenly enthronement (Acts 2:6–11, 32, 33).

Peter’s three denials, predicted by Jesus (vv. 34, 35), are recorded in all four Gospels (Mark 14:66–72; Luke 22:54–62; John 18:15–18, 25–27), although the accounts differ in certain details. Peter’s oaths (vv. 72, 74) mean that he appealed to God to witness to something that was not true (see 5:33–37; Ex. 20:7). The fact that all the Gospels record this incident shows how deeply it impressed the mind of the early church. It is a testimony to both human weakness and the greatness of God’s mercy, for Jesus restores and uses Peter despite his shameful failure (Luke 22:31, 32; John 21:15–19).

Judas’s remorse is not the same as repentance (3:2 note). Paul contrasts godly grief that “produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret” with “worldly grief” that “produces death” (2 Cor. 7:10). Judas’s regret, devoid of faith in God’s mercy, is very different from the repentant grief that brings Peter to restoration through repentance (26:75).

They cannot claim indifference to the question of “innocent blood” for which they paid the price (26:15), as they acknowledge in deciding not to return the funds to the temple treasury (27:6). This attempt at passing responsibility is no more effective than Pilate’s in v. 24.
See note on Acts 1:18.

Most of the words in the quotation are from Zech. 11:12, 13, but the content is also closely related to Jer. 19:1–13, a prophecy of judgment for the shedding of innocent blood (Jer. 19:4). Jeremiah twice speaks of a potter (Jer. 19:1, 11), and Matthew’s “Field of Blood” recalls his designation of Tophet as the “Valley of Slaughter” (Jer. 19:6), which also was to become a burial ground (Jer. 19:11). The actions of Judas and the priests are a fulfillment of the judgment prophecies of Zechariah and Jeremiah.
Jesus again (26:64) affirms the truth that He is king of the Jews, making Pilate a witness to His identity while suggesting that the governor’s understanding of the title may be incomplete at best.
Jesus’ silence fulfills Is. 53:7. See note on 26:63.

Unlike the dreams associated with Jesus’ birth (1:20; 2:12, 13, 19, 22), the nightmare suffered by Pilate’s wife is not explicitly said to have been sent by God. Yet the implication is that God has shown this Gentile woman Jesus’ innocence, and therefore Pilate should listen and learn from her dream and testimony that Jesus is a righteous man.

When Pilate seems reluctant to act, the people are not afraid to say that they will take the responsibility themselves. Their guilt, and that of Pilate and Judas, is not determined by them but by God (cf. Acts 4:27). According to Ezekiel, descendants do not share the guilt of their parents unless they cooperate in their sins (Ezek. 18:20; cf. Acts 2:23, 39).
The Roman scourge was a multi-stranded whip with bits of bone tied to the ends. Prisoners often died from this punishment.

Lit. “cloak,” of a Roman soldier. The cheap dye used in military uniforms apparently turned this cloth maroon, which could be called either “scarlet” (Matthew) or “purple” (Mark and John). The reddish cloak, crown of thorns, and reed placed in Jesus’ hand as a scepter costumes Jesus for the ceremony wherein the soldiers mock His acceptance of the title “King of the Jews.” As the Jewish authorities have ridiculed His prophetic calling (26:67), so Gentile forces ridicule His royal calling.

Crucifixion was a slow and agonizing death. Nails were probably driven through the wrists rather than the palms of the hands. The weight of the suspended body made breathing difficult and painful. Involuntary efforts by the legs to ease the pressure greatly increased pain in the feet. This ordeal continued until the exhausted victim could no longer breathe and more often than not, this process took several days.

**27:32 a man of Cyrene, Simon.** Ordinarily, convicts were forced to carry or drag the horizontal bar of their cross to the place of execution, compounding their humiliation and suffering (10:38). After the agony and blood loss of His flogging, Jesus may have lacked the strength to do so. Mark 15:21 names Simon’s sons, probably implying that they are known to Mark’s readers, perhaps as members of the church to which that gospel was addressed (see Rom. 16:13). The naming of Simon suggests that he, too, was known to Matthew’s audience, having subsequently become a Christian. Cyrene was in Libya, northern Africa, raising the question of whether Simon was a Jew from the dispersion or a Gentile pressed into the Savior’s service.

Any of several bitter herbs; Mark mentions myrrh. Commentators often note that myrrh mixed with wine is a painkiller. But the offer of galled wine is probably not a gesture of compassion but of mockery, as in Ps. 69:21. Jesus’ thirst is certainly great at this point, but the gall makes the wine undrinkable. If He tastes anesthetic in the wine, His refusal here near the beginning of the crucifixion may be motivated by a resolution to endure its anguish with undiminished consciousness and sensitivity to pain.
This action fulfills Ps. 22:18, as is made explicit in John 19:23, 24. The events surrounding the crucifixion of Jesus include numerous fulfillments of Ps. 22.
The placard at the head of the cross specifies the crime. Pilate is insulting the Jewish leaders (Mark 15:12), but the irony of its truth would be apparent to the early church.

The term translated “robbers” is the word Josephus uses for rebels. Mere thieves were not ordinarily crucified, so perhaps these two were conspirators in the violent insurrection led by Barabbas (Mark 15:7).

Again note the irony. Jesus _will_ return after three days and “rebuild” the temple of His body (John 2:19–22). Precisely because He is the Son of God, He will not come down from the cross, and in order to save others, He will not save Himself (v. 42).

Unwittingly, the mockers echo Ps. 22:8, ignoring the psalm’s forecast of God’s deliverance of the faithful sufferer (vv. 22–31). Jesus entrusts Himself to God (1 Pet. 2:23), who answers His plea for deliverance from death by His resurrection (Heb. 5:7).
Later that afternoon, one repents and expresses faith in Jesus, who promises him entrance into Paradise (Luke 23:40–43).

verse_quote: from the sixth hour ... until the ninth hour.
note: From noon to three p.m.

Jesus’ desolate cry is a fulfillment of Ps. 22:1, showing the depth of His distress as He suffers separation from His Father. Later, the apostles realize that Jesus was at this point enduring the dreadful wrath of God’s judgment on sin. This is all the more agonizing for one whose relationship with the Father is perfect in love. The cry is Aramaic, except the Hb. “Eli.” Mark gives the Aramaic “Eloi.”
The offer of sour wine to quench Jesus’ thirst fulfills Ps. 69:21 (v. 34 note)., 49
Apparently He cries, “It is finished!” (a single word in Greek; John 19:30).

The curtain of the temple separates the Most Holy Place from the outer chamber, in which priests serve daily. This curtain symbolizes God’s unapproachable holiness, since the high priest alone can pass through it, and only on the Day of Atonement (Heb. 9:7, 8). Jesus’ death is His sacrifice at the heavenly altar (Heb. 9:12, 24, 25), which opens the way for believers to approach God (Heb. 10:19, 20). Heaven has been opened through the royal priesthood and conscience-purifying sacrifice of Christ (1 Pet. 2:9).

**from top to bottom.** Through Jesus’ death, God Himself creates access into His presence, which formerly was sequestered in the Most Holy Place, the innermost part of Israel’s temple. Jesus has begun to become the true end-time temple even during His ministry (cf. John 2:19–22); therefore, it makes sense that His death—to which the Day of Atonement sacrifices in the Most Holy Place pointed—and His resurrection convey God’s very presence to those who trusted in Him. This presence, formerly limited to Israel’s old temple, even embraces Gentiles, as is evident from the Roman centurion watching at the cross, who acknowledges Jesus as “the Son of God” (27:54).

The resurrection of the “many ... saints” apparently occurs when the temple curtain is torn and the earth shakes at Jesus’ death, although their appearance to many in Jerusalem awaited Jesus’ resurrection on the third day. This resurrection, like those performed by Jesus during His ministry (9:23, 24; John 11:41–44), anticipates the general resurrection prophesied in Dan. 12:2. Since 1 Cor. 15:23 distinguishes Christ’s resurrection as firstfruits from that of believers “at his coming,” it is likely that these saints are returned only temporarily to life in mortal bodies (only to die again) for the sake of demonstrating that Jesus’ death has inaugurated the new creation.

verse_quote: Truly this was the Son of God.
note: Although they may not have understood fully the phrase they used, these Gentile soldiers make an appropriate confession of Jesus’ identity, as Simon Peter did on behalf of the rest of the apostles (16:16 and note; see 3:17; 17:5), while the natural heirs of the covenant are deriding their Messiah.

Joseph’s gift of a tomb completes Jesus’ fulfillment of Is. 53:9. See note on Luke 23:50, 51. Although the disciples closest to Jesus fled at His arrest (26:56) and Peter denied knowing Jesus (26:69–75), Joseph acts as a true disciple of Jesus by arranging for His burial, as the disciples of John the Baptist did for him (14:12).

Matthew includes this as background for 28:11–15 (see note).

**27:62 next day.** The Sabbath. See note on John 19:14.

verse_quote: the first day of the week.
note:
Jesus’ resurrection implicitly sanctifies the first day of the week as the new day of worship, replacing the seventh-day Sabbath for the new covenant people of God (John 20:1, 19, 26; Acts 20:7; 1 Cor. 16:2). Early Christians referred to it as “the Lord’s day” (Rev. 1:10).

**went to see the tomb.** Other gospels report that they bring spices to prepare Jesus’ body for burial more adequately than was possible before the Sabbath started at sundown two days earlier (Mark 16:1; Luke 24:1).

verse_quote: took hold of his feet and worshiped him.
note: As a result of His resurrection, Jesus’ body is not subject to corruption (1 Cor. 15:42–44); however, it is material and therefore touchable (Luke 24:39–42; see John 20:17). The women’s worship of Jesus corresponds to Thomas’s confession, “My Lord and my God,” which he makes upon touching Jesus’ wounds (John 20:28).
Jesus calls all His disciples “my brothers” (12:49, 50; 25:40), but here the reference is to the apostles, who will soon see Him in Galilee (see Mark 16:7; Luke 24:9).

Although the Jewish leaders did not believe Jesus’ predictions that He would rise on the third day, they now treat them more seriously and move to cover up what has happened. Soldiers posted to guard the tomb against Jesus’ disciples become “like dead men” in their terror when the angel of the Lord descends to remove the stone from the empty tomb of the risen, living Lord Jesus (28:3). The glorious, stunning appearance of the angel of the Lord (vv. 3, 4) appears to have had no effect on those committed to unbelief. For a price and a promise of immunity from punishment for sleeping on their watch, the soldiers readily perjure themselves. That the story of the disciples’ stealing Jesus’ body was still circulated in the days of Justin Martyr (c. 160 A.D.) suggests the Jewish leaders’ desperation to explain the indisputable fact of Jesus’ empty tomb.

As the women experienced both “fear and great joy” when they carried the angel’s announcement that Jesus had risen, so some among the eleven disciples respond to His unexpected but undeniable appearance with doubt (cf. Luke 24:11, 22, 23, 36–41). The initial reaction of disbelief on the part of those who will become bold eyewitnesses to Jesus’ resurrection shows that the proofs He offers are completely convincing (Acts 1:3), overwhelming their every misgiving.

Jesus now has “all authority.” The Son of Man has come before the Ancient of Days and has received everlasting dominion over “all peoples, nations, and languages” (Dan. 7:13, 14). The last stage of history has begun, as will soon be seen and heard when Jesus pours out the Holy Spirit from His heavenly throne (Acts 2:32, 33; 26:64 note). It will not be completed until Christ comes again in glory (Rev. 1:7).

The Great Commission is given on Christ’s mediatorial authority. Since Christ’s dominion is universal, the gospel must go to the whole world. This commandment is the primary reason for evangelism and missions.

**make disciples.** As the explanatory verbs “baptizing” and “teaching” indicate, the process of making disciples includes both evangelism of unbelievers—in which they are called to repentance and faith and submission to baptism, the sign of inclusion in the new covenant—and the instruction of believers in a life conformed to Jesus’ commandments, in response to His saving grace.

**nations.** The same Gk. word is often translated “Gentiles.” The great promise that in Abraham all the nations will be blessed (Gen. 12:3) is ready to be fulfilled (Matt. 1:1; 8:11).

**baptizing them.** See note on 3:6. Those who become disciples are baptized in (lit. “into”) God’s triune name. There is one name (not “names”), and one baptism; Father, Son, and Spirit are three distinct persons in the Godhead, and these three are one God. Disciples are baptized “in” this name because they belong to God, having been brought into the new covenant that expresses the will of the triune God. See theological note “The Sacraments.”

Disciples are not just taught what to believe but also how to obey. Jesus taught practical holiness, as Matthew showed in the Sermon on the Mount (chs. 5–7), in Jesus’ instruction on relationships among believers (ch. 18), and elsewhere.

**I am with you always.** Jesus was named Immanuel (“God with us”) at His birth (1:23), and now He promises to be with His disciples to the end of the age, as the Lord had promised His presence to OT figures such as Jacob (Gen. 28:15) and Joshua (Josh. 1:5–9) and to Israel as a whole (Is. 43:5). He is with them specifically in the responsibility of teaching His will to the world.

**to the end of the age.** As the promise of Christ’s presence extends beyond the apostles’ life spans, so the disciple-making commission first spoken to the Eleven is now entrusted to the church, which is founded on the apostles’ confession (16:16–18).
